The *Kāmakalāvilāsa* composed by Puṇyānanda: Salutations to Śiva, the Lord, whose form is consciousness and whose nature is bliss.
Salutations to the illustrious one, whose tremulous side-glances shatter the fear of all afflictions.
I bow to that divine couple, the primordial mass of bliss and consciousness,
who are praised by the wise as the unsurpassed, supreme light.
Salutations to the venerable Naṭanānanda-yogin, the Supreme Self, the Guru whose splendor is a mixture of red and white light. || 3 ||
Bow with supreme devotion to Nāthānanda, who is the bliss of the awakening to the identity of consciousness;
who is the hidden meaning of the Upaniṣads, and who is seated upon the auspicious throne of the bliss of all beings.
From the lord of sages, Puṇyānanda, there was born the renowned Kāmakalā; Naṭanānanda provides a certain commentary on her name. (5)

For here indeed are the venerable Puṇyānandas, who are experts in determining the purport of all the Vedas and Vedāntas as they blossom forth through the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*); who are proficient in the true tradition (*satsampradāya*);

who know the reality of the Self as it is determined by the meaning of all the Āgamas; who are adept at sporting in the ocean of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*); who, manifesting the Supreme Self for themselves, have entered into the Supreme Lord as their own self, and [lead] others [to do the same].
With the desire to uplift those persons who possess devotion, [the author] prays for protection characterized by oneness with the Supreme Self:

"May Maheśa protect me—he whose play consists of the effortless sport of the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of the entire universe; in whom all reflective awareness is inwardly absorbed; and whose body is pure luminosity alone. (1)

In this *Cidvallī*, Puṇyānandayogin— whose multitude of all bonds has been shaken off by the compassionate side-glances of his supreme guru, who was satisfied by his natural devotion through the power of his merit—

desiring to explain the sequence of worship for the mantra-cycle of Mahātripurasundarī, the presiding deity of all sciences (*vidyā*), first describes her form as Kāmakāmeśvarī, who is her very locus of manifestation.

Regarding the passage beginning with *sakala*: the "arising" (*udaya*) of all worlds is their origination; "subsistence" (*sthiti*) is their preservation; and "dissolution" (*laya*) is their destruction. This triad is indicative of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*). Just as the process of "triple-making" (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is indicative of "fivefold-making" (*pañcīkaraṇa*), [this triad indicates the full range of His activity]. That which abounds in these fivefold functions is "sport" (*līlā*); "delight" (*vinodana*) is play (*krīḍana*). He who is intent upon that, who is ever-watchful (*jāgarūka*), is the subject. I have employed the suffix *maya* here in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).

It is like [the expression] "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*), and not like "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*) in such contexts. Why? Because the fivefold activity (*pañcavidhakṛtya*) is indeed an effect residing in the universe (*jagat*), whereas divine play (*līlā*) resides in the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Therefore, in this context, by the term *bhuvana* qualified by the word *sakala*, the entire collection of principles (*tattvajāta*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth (*dharaṇī*)—that from which things come into being—is denoted. Since these principles have arisen from Brahman, they reside within Him.

Because it abides [therein] and because of its dissolution into that very [reality]. And thus says the Taittirīya Śruti: "That from which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter when they depart—desire to know that; that is Brahman. By the word "exerted," [the text refers to] the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; one only, without a second, Brahman."

"The multiverse (prapañca) residing within Himself [thought], 'May I become many; may I procreate. Then He made Himself by Himself"—by this it is stated that He became intent upon a creation characterized by such a volition (saṅkalpa).

Likewise, the Rahasyagurus state: "The Lord, whose very nature is consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects externally—without any material cause—by the power of His will, just as a yogi does. For this very reason, the creation of the world and so forth by the Lord is merely a sport (*līlā*); there is no other motive.

And so says the *Hṛdayasūtra*: "By its own will, it unfolds the universe upon its own wall. Likewise, there is also this statement: "By its own will alone, it swallows and also emits the entire world.
The *Śruti* also says: "As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]. There is yet another statement:
"Having painted the variegated world within itself by means of the brush of its own will..."
Having beheld it himself, the Supreme Lord rejoices.

And thus, Maheśvara alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the production of the universe, according to the scriptural text regarding his becoming manifold: "May I become many. This is also because of the denial of any other substratum in the text: "One only, without a second. Furthermore, in the *Pratyabhijñā-sūtra*—in the statement, "Consciousness itself, having ascended to the state of the cognizer..."—by the phrase "the uncontracted consciousness," it is stated that the Supreme Self alone has assumed the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Scripture also says: "By this..."
"Having entered by means of the living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest name and form," he said. Likewise, in the *Lalitopākhyāna* as well:
"Though residing in the hearts of the worlds, she is invisible and delusive in nature;
she effects the differentiation of names and forms through her own play."
And in the *Catuḥśatikā*:

"When this has been fully transformed, nothing at all is perceived. Such a web of traditional texts (*smṛti*) should be cited. Likewise, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Have you then asked for that instruction, my dear, by which the unheard becomes heard..."

Having proposed that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all—stating, "What is heard becomes known; what is thought becomes known; what is not cognized becomes cognized"—the text provides an illustration through such statements as:
"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth. From this, it is established that Brahman itself, having transformed into those various forms, manifests therein.
Now, by this much of the section, it has been stated that the world is non-different from the essential nature of Brahman. And this being so...

In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of Brahman is—characterized as being distinct from the world—the author says: "The internalized reflection," and so forth. *Vimarśa* (reflection) is that which is reflected upon or perceived as "this," namely the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For the well-known conceptual reference of the universe created by the Supreme Self is precisely "this. Thus, the Śruti begins with, "From the Self, space was born," and continues... [the rest of the citation follows].

Having described the creation of the body with the words, "Or rather, this person consists of the essence of food," the text continues with the passage, "Of this, this is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk; this is the tail, the support," and so forth; for in such statements, there is indeed observed a reference to the manifold world (*prapañca*) through the identification of "this is this. Furthermore, in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:

"I am effecting the dissolution of this [world], which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of 'this' (*idam*). Thus, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which has Brahman as its counter-correlate, is designated by the term "this. One whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is of such a nature—that is, one in whom the reflective awareness of the phenomenal world is dissolved within or internalized—is called "one whose reflective awareness is internally dissolved" (*antarlīnavimarśa*). The meaning, therefore, is: one who has assimilated the entire phenomenal world into his own self.
"I am the Supreme Self, whose nature is the supreme light of ultimate bliss, free from fear due to the cultivation of the realization of my full perfection.

This will be elaborated upon later in the section on the determination of the meaning of "I"; however, something is said here as well by way of incidental discussion. One becomes possessed of supreme bliss through the realization that "Brahman is I. Thus says the Upaniṣad: "Therefore, indeed, different from this [self] consisting of consciousness, there is another inner..."

Having pointed out the Supreme Self with the words, "The Self consists of bliss," the text continues: "Joy is its head; delight is its right wing; great delight is its left wing; bliss is the self; Brahman is the tail, the support. Thus, it speaks of the Supreme Brahman as characterized by the fullness of *ahantā* (I-ness). Now, one might object: by the statement "bliss is the self," the nature of the self as being bliss is established.
However, it is not [merely] the state of being qualified by full *ahantā* (I-consciousness); how then can it be said that the Supreme Brahman is "qualified by full *ahantā*"?
Bliss (*ānanda*) is indeed the contemplation of the self-nature of the universe. Thus, in the *Subālopaniṣad*: "The elemental self consists of food; the sensory self consists of vital breath;

the mental self consists of volition; the cognitive self consists of time; the blissful self consists of dissolution (*laya*). Here, "dissolution" (*laya*) refers to the contemplation of full *ahambhāvanā*.
Regarding the statement as well—"Absorption (laya) is equal to ten million meditations"—this is the explanation given here concerning "the Supreme, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss.

This was explained by Amṛtānanda Yogin in this way, because he stated that "consciousness (cit) is the digit of pure awareness (caitanyakalā), and bliss (ānanda) is the transformation into universal I-consciousness (viśvāhantā)."
Alternatively, *vimarśa* is the non-artificial awareness of the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*), which serves as the cause for the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.

Likewise, the *Nāgānanda* states: "Vimarśa (reflective awareness) is the unartificial flash of 'I am,' whether by way of the manifestation of the universe, the illumination of the universe, or the withdrawal of the universe. To be absorbed in that [awareness] means being inward-turned (*antarmukhatva*). And thus the meaning is: he whose reflective awareness is inwardly absorbed and turned inward is one for whom there is the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāvanā*). Likewise, in the venerable *Svacchandaśāstra*:
"But that internal state which is the locus of qualities such as omniscience—could its loss ever occur? For nothing else is perceived. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"That light which is the self of the universe, capable of illuminating both itself and others, is called the one 'I';
such is its state as 'I-ness' (ahantā). Thus [it is said]. Śivānanda Svāmin also [states]:
"I am [the one] who pervades the entire three worlds without being overcome by fatigue.

Thus, he states that such Supreme Brahman, the Parameśvara, has the nature of pure luminosity (*prakāśa*) and is superior to all, saying: "The Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) whose body is pure luminosity alone"—that is, a body (*tanuḥ*) not distinct from luminosity itself. And so it is said in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
"That light which shines beyond this heaven,
that the gods worship as the light of lights, as life and as immortality.
"This very self, endowed with serene joy, having risen up from this body and having attained the supreme light, appears in its own true form."

Thus [it is said]: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. And likewise, the Rahasyāgama states:
"The inner light of one's own nature is indeed the non-departing Parāvāk."

"I salute the unsurpassed Light. And also in the *Parāpañcāśikā*: "The one Śa [Śiva] is within this Light; his are both the splendors and the darknesses. Also in the *Saubhāgyahṛdaya*: "I bow to that supreme Greatness," and so forth. Here, what is called "luminosity" (*prakāśatva*) is the "I" whose nature is the vibration inherent within the first person—expressed as "I will," "I know," and "I act."

It is indeed *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness). Consequently, it is stated that the Supreme Brahman is that which is endowed with the five powers consisting of omniscience, omnipresence, universal agency, fullness, and pervasiveness. Now, an objection may be raised: "The quality of being an illuminator is observed even in the case of the sun and other luminaries; how then can this [Brahman] alone possess the nature of the supreme illuminator? To this, he says: "Maheśa. That is, He is the Great Lord (*maheśa*), meaning He is both great (*mahān*) and the Lord (*īśa*). His greatness (*mahattva*) consists in His having a nature that is unconditioned by space, time, or form.

And "lordship" (īśatva) is the state of being the controller of all. Thus, the Yajurvedic scripture—having pointed out that Brahman is unlimited in every respect with the words, "From which speech turns back"—declares:
"This is His supreme divine [power], eager for the self-awareness of its own nature."
She is the fullness of all existents, wherein there is neither deficiency nor excess.

It says: "Likewise, in the Atharva-veda Upaniṣad: 'Now, for what reason is he called Maheśvara? Because he seizes up, creates, emits, and causes all the worlds to dwell; therefore he is called Maheśvara. Also in another Upaniṣad:
'The sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda...'"
Of that which is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti), he who is beyond it is the Great Lord (Maheśvara).

"From fear of him the wind blows," and so forth; "By the command of this Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart," and so forth. Likewise, the *Pratyakṣopaniṣad* states: "That which is the Supreme Brahman is that one Rudra; he is Īśāna, he is the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, he is Mahādeva. Also, in the *Parāpañcāśikā*:
He alone is the Supreme Lord, the essential nature of all beings;
He alone is the god Bhairava, characterized by the sustaining of the universe.
Having thus pointed out the Supreme Lord— this is His very own supreme Goddess, eager for the self-reflection of His own nature,
in whom there is neither too little nor too much of the fullness of all existents.
Having thus established the union of the Supreme Self with the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti), who is His own complete form— this Lord, ever eager for the flavor of play with this Goddess,
the Sovereign, simultaneously ordains manifold creations and dissolutions.
The capacity to accomplish that which is exceedingly difficult to achieve is indeed his unsurpassed nature;
this very sovereignty is what is designated as supreme autonomy.

Thus, having correctly delineated the nature of Brahman, it has been explained: "In this way, the venerable Supreme Lord, accompanied by the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), is the Lord of all, the Sovereign of beings, the Protector of beings, the bridge and the upholder; for the sake of the non-confusion of these worlds.
According to the manner stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, may the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self—the protector of all in every respect—protect you.

Those meritorious persons, endowed with boundless compassion and blissful through their merit, offer their aspirations for [the welfare of] virtuous men; and here, protection consists precisely in the state of oneness with the Supreme Self. Thus, in the *Cidvilāsa*: "In this world, deliverance from the peril of the adversary characterized by duality is the supreme self-protection. By this, contemplation through non-duality is intended. And this is the underlying intention of those whose bliss is merit: that here, the Supreme Self alone is the friend of all beings.
In this world, having assumed the form of a true guru, he protects a few who are devoted to him.
The *Yajurveda* says: "And that lineage of teachers is to be known as 'this one, that one,' [extending] back to the Blessed One.
"A man who has a teacher knows; the teacher, indeed, shall tell you the way. "For you are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore of ignorance.
"Having examined the worlds acquired through action, a Brahmin should attain detachment, for there is nothing uncreated to be gained by what is created."
"For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*).

This collection of scriptural passages, beginning thus, declares that the attainment of Brahman occurs through the means of approaching a venerable Guru (*śrīgurūpasadana*). And as the *Āgama* states:
"From the auspicious conjunction of Śiva and Śakti performed in a previous birth..."
When there is equilibrium of karma, one's contemplation should be focused on the worship of Śiva.
"Then Śiva himself, having directly assumed the form of the Guru, the Soul of the Universe, bestows initiation through the penetration of Śambhu’s power. And the Gītā says:
"Know that through prostration, through inquiry, and through service;

the wise who perceive reality will instruct you in knowledge. And there is this statement by an authoritative teacher: "By taking refuge in the glance of a compassionate and auspicious guide, the *śāmbhavavedha* initiation occurs through his compassion."

And it should be contemplated as having come down through the lineage succession of the two stages beginning with Paramaśiva. In this regard, something is stated by way of digression: by the words, "May Maheśa, whose body is pure light, protect [us]," the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra is established. How so? Because the Teacher (Ācārya) indeed possesses the quality of being the illuminator. Thus says the Sūtra: "Likewise, the Guru is the means. And likewise, the author of its commentary [the Vṛtti] also says: "He who instructs..."

The Guru reveals the reality (*tattva*) and the pervasiveness (*vyāpti*) of the hymn; therefore, he is proclaimed as the "means" (*upāya*). [The syllable] *ṅgha* signifies protection, for even a mantra possesses the quality of protecting. The etymological meaning of the word *mantra* is "that which protects through contemplation" (*mananāt trāyate*). And according to the scripture: "Mantras are said to be those whose nature is to protect through contemplation. The *Śivasūtra* also states: "The mind is in the mantra," indicating that the mantra is the protector of consciousness.
This meaning is also established by the *Catuḥśatikā* in the section defining the sixfold sequence (*athaṣaṭka*), regarding the subjects known as the *nigarbha*:
"O Great Goddess, the *nigarbha* meaning has as its scope Śiva, the Guru, and the Self; O Mistress of the Gods, I shall describe its method to you in mere outline."
"Having realized that even the Guru possesses the same nature as Śiva, the partless reality,
one attains the state of being Śiva through the power of beholding Him and [realizing] one's own self as Śiva.
With this intention, our most excellent teacher, the venerable Guru Śaṅkarānanda, has also correctly determined:
"Salutation to Śiva, the Lord, whose form is consciousness and whose form is bliss;
to the illustrious one, who has shattered the fear of affliction with the tremulous glance of his sidelong glances," and so forth.
Likewise, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:

"For one who has supreme devotion to God, and as to God so to the Guru, these truths declared here shine forth to that high-souled one. Thus, it is only by the Māheśvaras belonging to the true lineage (*satsampradāya*) that the Self, which is Kāmeśvara, is attained, and not by others; enough of this.
Having followed this digression, let us return to the subject at hand.

Now, one might ask: how can this Self be said to be the Supreme Lord Paramaśiva alone as the creator of all, given that His status as the creator of all is heard to be denied? For it is indeed heard in scripture: "Neither His activity nor His instrument exists; there is none equal to Him, nor any superior to Him; His supreme power is heard to be truly manifold. It is precisely through connection with the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) that His status as the creator of all and His superiority over all [is established].

For it is heard that the entire universe originates from Parābhaṭṭārikā alone, preceded by her feet. Moreover: "That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (svadhayā)"; "By faith the god attains godhood," and so forth; and there is the traditional teaching of the learned: "Your one form, O Śā [Śakti], triumphs as the witness. Furthermore, it is because the existence of this Maheśvara is heard of only through the proximity of Parābhaṭṭārikā.
It is true that the Lord’s status as the sole creator of all and so forth does not cohere [if considered in isolation].
For we do not say that the Supreme Lord, Paramaśiva, is a solitary agent devoid of Parābhaṭṭārikā;
rather, having determined that reality consists of the very nature of Śiva and Śakti, we have declared His causality.
Likewise, there is the statement of an authoritative source: "The wise indeed declare that Śiva and Śakti are one single reality."

In the *Śrī Svacchanda* as well: "The Lord Śiva, established in the principles (*tattva*), is the supreme cause; Śiva is the agent of all, and this Power (*śakti*) is said to be the cause. Thus, the agency of both is declared. In that very same text:
"The Supreme Power, non-different from Śiva, is the embodiment of all actions."
Through the divisions of Vāmā, Icchā, and so forth, she has attained the state of the three couples.

According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), there is only one cause of the universe; otherwise, a contradiction with the *śruti* would result. [The *śruti* states: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), thus establishing its oneness. Therefore, the statement that Śiva is the cause applies equally to Śakti as well. For this very reason, the agency attributed to Śakti is likewise equal to that of Śiva.
The Goddess is not without Śiva, nor is Śiva without the Goddess;
there is no difference whatsoever between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.
Thus, according to the established tenets of the Āgama, he declares that even the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) is the cause of all:
Victorious is that primordial Power, whose nature is eternal and incomparable, consisting of her own innate bliss;
she is the seed of the future moving and unmoving world, and a stainless mirror for the reflective awareness of the form of Śiva. (2)
The "Cidvallī" [declares]:
"Victorious is that primordial power, the undivided Supreme Bhaṭṭārikā Mahātripurasundarī, who exists with supreme excellence.
She alone consists of the entire phenomenal universe, comprising the thirty-six principles from Śiva down to Earth, and yet she transcends them; this is well-known in all the Upaniṣads."

She is called Tripurā. Indeed, this is how the etymology of the word "Tripurā" is performed by great yogis who are knowers of the true tradition: "She is Tripurā because she existed prior to (purā) the three—fire, water, and earth. For it is precisely her existence prior to fire, water, and earth that constitutes Brahman's transcendence of all principles (tattvas), and through that, her nature as the essence of all principles; the Upaniṣads also declare this very same thing.

Likewise, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "There was Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi; his father said to him, 'Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). Having thus enjoined upon his son the life of a student consisting of the study of the Vedas and so forth, [the text continues]: 'Having approached [his teacher] at twelve years of age, having studied all the Vedas at twenty-four years of age, he returned, high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant. His father said to him, "Are you indeed arrogant?"'"

"Ask him for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. Having ascertained the disciple's fitness through these words and others, the teacher imparted the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). In that context, it was stated that through the knowledge of one thing, all things are known, thereby expressing that all principles (*tattva*) are identical with That. Desiring an illustration for this, the disciple asks: "How indeed, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about?"

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known— the modification being a mere matter of name, a verbal handle, while the reality is simply 'clay'"— through such a succession of illustrations, [the text] establishes that the Supreme Brahman is both the soul of the universe and transcendent to it; and subsequently, through passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," it [establishes] that which transcends the universe.

Having first denoted the entity, it then denotes that which has the universe as its self: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. Having so resolved, it emitted heat; [having emitted] heat, water, and food, this very deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate name and form; let me make each of them threefold. This very deity, having entered these three deities with this living self, differentiated name and form. Regarding those [deities], it made each one threefold. This very deity, having entered these three deities with this living self, differentiated name and form.

By the passage beginning, "He made each of them threefold," it is stated that Brahman’s own essential nature consists in its being the antecedent of all and its filling all things through the non-egoistic state (*anahaṃbhāva*) of fire, water, and food; thus, it declares that the entire web of principles (*tattvajāla*), from the gods down to stationary objects, is composed of nothing but fire, water, and food. This is just as [the Chāndogya Upaniṣad] states: "The modification of firewood into fire is a mere verbal handle, a name; the truth is simply the three forms," and so forth, regarding the food that is eaten.
"It is divided threefold: that which is its grossest constituent becomes feces; that which is middling becomes flesh; that which is subtlest becomes the mind," and so forth.
Thus, because it fills the triply-constituted phenomenal world (*trivṛtkṛta-prapañca*), the Supreme Brahman itself is designated as the "Tripura" (the Triple City).
The author expresses this very same point later in the text:
"Vidyā consists of the thirty-six principles and is also the absolute (kevalā) that transcends the principles.
Thus [it is said]. Smṛti also states: "The Heart of the Supreme Lord is both the soul of the universe and that which transcends it.
And in the venerable Vāmakeśvaratantra as well:

"Tripurā is the supreme power, the primordial Maheśvarī who has come forth; she is the Mother (Mātṛkā) of the origin of the three worlds through her division into the gross and the subtle, whose essential nature consists of the entire multitude of principles (tattvas) swallowed up without remainder. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Śrīsvacchanda*:
"Here there is no time, no absence of *kalās*, no unity, and no deity;
it is the supreme reality of perfect liberation, which is called the mouth of Rudra."
O lady of beautiful hips, behold that which is known as Śiva-Śakti— free from conceptual construction, stainless, beyond the visible, and wondrously transcending both speech and mind.
"Partless and yet with parts, formless and free from conceptual construction,
beyond dualities— the supreme reality known as Śiva, the highest state.
And in our own *Saccidānandavāsanā*:
I enter as my own self the Goddess who is the soul of all, yet transcends them, whose nature is light and awareness, and who consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme.

Thus, in various places throughout numerous *Śrutis*, *Smṛtis*, and other texts, the supreme excellence of Tripurā is proclaimed. He explains this very point with the phrase "she whose form is eternally incomparable and consisting of her own bliss": *nija* means natural or inherent; *sukhamaya* means having the nature of bliss unmixed with suffering;
*nitya* means eternal or existing at all times; *nirupama* means peerless, having no equal or superior; *ākāra* means whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is such. This is the meaning.

"—is of the nature of infinite, uncreated self-bliss. Likewise, the Upaniṣad begins: "If this entire earth were filled with his wealth, that would be one human bliss," and continues through a sequence of successively increasing hundredfold increments—from humans up to the four-faced Brahmā—presenting a succession of blisses for various beings, concluding: "That is one bliss of Brahman; he who..."

"That which is in this person and that which is in yonder sun are one"—this declares the all-pervasive nature and the transcendence of the Brahman of supreme bliss. Furthermore, in another Upaniṣad, after stating, "The Infinite alone is happiness; the Infinite indeed is what one must seek to understand," it is heard that Brahman consists of unlimited bliss: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite. Likewise:
And other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss; thus, it is said that all others are but droplets from the ocean of Brahman-bliss.
In the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, in the *Catuḥśatī*:
"I bow to the Great Goddess, whose form is supreme bliss."
Even today, the gods do not know even the slightest bit about her.

"The Supreme is a mass of eternal bliss. Thus, it is the peerless state of eternal bliss, stainless and free from conceptual construction; its very nature is the flowing nectar of happiness and awakening, overflowing with the weight of joy from the abundance of supreme bliss.

Thus, by the statement of the learned, "She who bestows the good fortune of the state filled with supreme bliss," and so forth, it is determined that Tripurā is of the nature of *sac-cid-ānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss). She is the seed of the future moving and non-moving; that is to say, she is the womb, the source, and the cause of the future moving and non-moving, the stationary and the animate. As the Yajurveda Śruti says: "He who is the first among the gods, who stands in the east, Rudra, who transcends all, the great seer..."
Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born; may that God endow us with auspicious mindfulness. He is the maker of all, the knower of all, whose source is the Self;

he is the wise one, the ordainer of time, the possessor of qualities, and the knower of all sciences. He who first creates Brahmā and who indeed sends forth the Vedas—he is the Lord of this world eternally, for no other cause is found for its governance. He is the one controller, the inner self of all beings; he is the single seed that becomes manifold.
The passage beginning with "he who performs" and so forth is to be understood here. And the scripture states:
"When that supreme power, by her own will, becomes the form of the universe and perceives her own radiance, then the manifestation of the *cakra* occurs."
Just as a great tree exists in the form of potential within the seed of a banyan,
so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the heart.
And in the *Lalitopākhyāna*:
"She who, at the beginning of creation, produced the Creator [Brahmā] filled with water. Also, in the *Parāvāsanā*:
Having herself painted the wondrous picture of the universe as her own form,
she beheld it herself and was filled with supreme wonder and satisfaction.
"Whose essential nature consists of the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) merged within the living subject (*jīva*) that is light.

Now, one might object: Śiva’s status as the creator of the universe would not be tenable without Śakti; likewise, the causality of the Supreme Śakti herself would not manifest without Paramaśiva. Therefore, how can it be said that she is "the seed of the future moving and unmoving world"? To this, he replies: "[She is] the stainless mirror of the reflective awareness whose form is Śiva."
Thus, the "I" (*aham*) is the very nature of Śiva; its *vimarśa* is its reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Reflective awareness is knowledge whose form is precisely "I.

In its manifestation, [Śiva] is like a stainless mirror, meaning he is perfectly adept at manifesting [it]. This is the meaning: just as a certain exceedingly beautiful king seated upon his throne clearly perceives the reflection of his own self in the surface of a clear mirror placed directly before him.

Having clearly perceived that reflection, one recognizes it as "this is I. In the same way, the Supreme Lord also, having correctly beheld His own power which is under His control, realizes His own true nature, thinking, "I am the Perfect One. And just as it would be impossible for a mirror to manifest a reflection within itself in the absence of a connection with an object situated before it, so too it is impossible for the Supreme Power to exist in the absence of a connection with Paramaśiva.

It follows by implication that the swallowing of the cosmic manifestation (*prapañca*) situated within one’s own heart is not possible [without the union of both]. Therefore, the world is not created by Śiva alone or by Śakti alone; rather, the entire collection of principles (*tattvajāta*) is projected by both Kāma and Kāmeśvara together.

As stated in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "He who alone is the wielder of the net, the Lord, rules over all worlds by his powers of ruling; he who alone exists at the time of emergence and dissolution."

"He who, being the one single color (caste), through the application of his power, bestows many colors while containing all meanings within himself—he who manifests the universe at the end and in the beginning—that God may unite us with auspicious intelligence. And as it has been said by the learned:
"He whose play consists of the rays of the world, which is bliss manifested by His own will..."
"I bow to the Great Seat of Consciousness (saṃvinmahāpīṭha), which takes refuge in the feet of Śiva and Śakti. Thus [it is said].
"We bow to that Śiva who, though his own nature is undivided, manifests the manifold conceptualization of the subject within the wheel of the maṇḍala of his own heart. Thus [ends verse] 2.

It has been determined that the Supreme Brahman is of the nature of "I" (aham) together with its power (śakti). Whatever needs to be said on this matter will be properly elaborated upon later; therefore, enough of this. Now, some indeed say that Brahman is devoid of reflective awareness (vimarśa); how then can it be said that Brahman possesses reflective awareness? To this, he says:

The Supreme Power (Parāśakti), whose form consists of the sprout of the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti, shines forth; her body is characterized by the script of the unsurpassed reflective awareness (vimarśa) in its most subtle form.

The meaning of this term *cidvallī* is as follows: here, by the word *parāśakti*, Mahātripurasundarī, known as *prakṛti*, is designated. She who is celebrated in the scriptures and well-known in the world as being of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) is described thus: "she whose form is the sprout of the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti"—and Śiva is...

*Śakti* refers to Śiva’s power (*śiva-śakti*), and their *samāgama* is their union. By this manifest (*sphuṭa*, i.e., evident) union of Śiva and Śakti, the web of principles (*tattva-jāla*)—ranging from the principle of Śiva down to the principle of Earth—is brought forth one after another, in the manner of a sprout from a seed and a seed from a sprout. In this context, by the word "Śiva," the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is denoted; and because the principle of Śiva is presided over by that power of knowledge, it is also [denoted] by the word "Śakti."

The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is designated [as such] because the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*), whose nature is consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda-svarūpinī*), is presided over by that power of action; for it is observed everywhere that the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-nirmāṇa*) occurs solely through knowledge and action. Thus, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "That which is seen here is the source of bliss; by it one lives. This has been declared: 'This supreme bliss is the source of enjoyment'; these two have form at will."

"The source of bliss is bliss; bliss is Brahman. This Goddess is indeed Brahman alone, who may be both one and manifold through the cosmic expansion (*prapañca*). She is of the nature of bliss in the fourth human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
And as it is said in the scripture:
"When that supreme power, by her own will, assumes the form of the universe..."
Then one should behold the emergence of the wheel from that vibrating self.

In the *Pratyabhijñāsūtra* as well, it is stated: "Consciousness (*citiḥ*) is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe. And there is the saying of the learned masters: "She is the source of all the gods and of all powers," and so forth. Thus, the meaning should be described as follows:
that very Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), becoming herself Śiva and Śakti, creates the universe. Accordingly, the Śruti says: "She who consists of the *liṅga*..."

"The cause of the state of being *nivīta* (the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder) by which this entire universe came into being at the beginning," and so forth, should be observed. Likewise, in the *Cidvilāsa*: "The circle of principles (*tattvacakra*) here, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva, is considered the supreme wheel. The deity who shines through the convention of her own essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the digit of consciousness (*sāṃvidī kalā*). She is described as the power of emission (*visargaśakti*), the cause of the universe. This has been explained in detail through reflection in the Vedānta known as the *Aitareya*."
Such is the statement of the learned. Furthermore, he qualifies that very [deity]: "She shines, her form being characterized by the script of supreme reflection (vimarśa) in its most subtle aspect.

She is *aṇutararūpā*, meaning she whose form (*rūpa*) is *aṇutara*—that is, extremely subtle. As the *Yajurveda* scripture states: "Thou art indeed that reality which is more subtle than the subtle, eternal; Thou art indeed that."
"That which is unseen, ungraspable," and so forth;
and: "This Self within the heart is subtler than a grain of rice or than a mustard seed."
Likewise, there is this statement:
"The Goddess is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.

Herein lies this supreme secret: the letter *a* is the alphabet of the Absolute (*anuttara*), and the letter *ha* is the alphabet of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By these two, the embodied form (*vigraha*) is indicated.

She whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is that [of the Absolute] is described as such. Here, by the phrase "the embodied form characterized by the script of the supreme reflective awareness" (*anuttaravimarśalipilakṣyavigraha*), the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*)—who is the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*) containing within her womb the entire collection of phonemes from *a* to *ha*, consisting of the fifty letters; who is the progenitor of the entire phenomenal world composed of phonemes, words, mantras, kalās, tattvas, and worlds; and who is the inner self of all beings—is seen everywhere in the Vedāntas as being perceived in the form of "I, I."

This is what has been stated. Likewise, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman. It knew only itself: 'I am Brahman. Also in the *Aitareya*: "'A' is Brahman; I have come to that. And in the *Tāpanīya*: "'Who are you? 'I,' he replied. 'It is exactly thus with all this. Therefore, "I" (ahaṃ) is the name for everything, and this letter 'a' is its beginning. He becomes that very [Brahman]."

"For this Self is indeed everything; for I am the inner Self of all, yet this entire world is not without Self; this whole universe is indeed the Self. Therefore, one should seek the Self, which is the Self of all, through a form that is the Self of all—this Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
In that very same place it is further stated: "Now, this Brahman is non-dual because of its vastness; it is eternal, pure, enlightened, free, real, and subtle."

Having thus described the Supreme Self as "the perfectly full, non-dual, Being-Consciousness-Bliss, which is pure Consciousness alone," he also states the method for its meditation: "For one who sees that which shines forth, which shines once and for all, which does not shine apart from all this [phenomenal world], the non-dual 'I am He (Haṃsaḥ So'ham)'—he becomes Brahman.

Whoever knows thus. This is the secret. The meditation on the Self, consisting of the cultivation of the state of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), is to be kept strictly hidden; it is to be understood only from the mouth of the Guru. Thus the Śruti itself declares.

Likewise, in the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with the words, "That [Being] thought; this divinity thought," and so forth, after describing Tripurā—the creator of the entire universe—who consists of the three forms of fire, water, and earth, it says: "Verily, that which is plenitude (bhūman) is bliss; where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is plenitude. Having thus pointed out her who is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, it begins with "She indeed is below," and concludes with "I am the Self."

"He points out: 'I alone am below, I am above, I am behind, I am in front, I am to the south, I am to the north—I indeed am all this. Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "'O venerable one, you are indeed I, O deity; you are indeed these deities, O venerable one,'" and so forth. Smṛti also says:
The Elders know that the letter *ha* is at the heart and the letter *a* is at the end of the twelve;
they are the single non-dual Self, which is the resting place within the light of consciousness.
"The letter 'A' is the foremost of all phonemes, the light, the supreme Śiva.
The final letter 'Ha' is the form of the creative power (kalā), proclaimed as reflective awareness (vimarśa).
That which is the state of perfect equilibrium between the two is clearly manifest as the Supreme 'I'. Thus it is said.
In the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā* as well:

"That light which is the self of the universe, capable of manifesting both itself and others, is called the one 'I'; alas, such is its state. One should reflect upon thousands of such statements; enough with excessive detail. || 3 ||

Henceforth, desiring to analyze the Kāmakalā, which is to be established through this treatise in the form of syllables, he begins to describe the nature of those syllables: "The Great Bindu enters the wall consisting of consciousness—which is as beautiful as a reflection, pure, and made of the mirror of self-awareness (vimarśa)—as the rays of the sun of Supreme Śiva reflect within it. (4)

From the beginning of the verse with "cidvallī" up to the end of "bindū dahanenduvigrahau," [it is described that] Paraśiva—the Lord Paraśiva whose sole nature is light—is indeed [the source]. The sun is the maker of days; its "karāḥ" are its rays. In that pure and stainless mirror of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), there is a mass (*nikara*), a cluster, of those [rays].
Vimarśa is the power of the manifestation of infinite forms. Thus, in the *Pratyabhijñā*, it is said: "She is that radiance," and so forth.
That very power is described as being like a mirror. Because it is the self-luminous manifestation of its own nature, "reflection" therein means the beholding of one's own nature.

When such reflection—the beholding of one's own nature—occurs within that which consists of consciousness, whose sole nature is knowledge, and which is beautiful with its own luster and delightful through its own radiance;
The Great Bindu enters the wall; having entered, it becomes manifest. This is because the determination of the wall-nature of the mind is the cause for the manifestation of the Great Bindu.

Even in the world, when one stands facing the sun, after the reflection of the sun's rays upon the surface of a mirror, a point of light—the concentrated brilliance of the sun's rays—is perceived directly on a nearby wall. In the same way, [it occurs] with the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light.

The meaning is that when the connection with the reflective awareness of one's own true nature occurs like a mirror, the Supreme Lord then manifests there in the form of the Great Bindu (mahābindu) as "I am full" (pūrṇo'ham). And likewise in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; one only, without a second. That Brahman thought: 'Let me be many,' and that deity thought. And also: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman."

Then, through the realization "I am Brahman," he beheld his own Self; he then contemplated: "Create these worlds. Thus, in such scriptural passages, the Supreme Brahman, which is oriented toward the contemplation of its own power, is called the cause of the universe. And the Āgama states:
"One should perceive the throbbing of the Self; then the manifestation of the Cakra occurs."
Also in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"That radiance is the Great Being, qualified by space and time;
it is said to be the very essence within the heart of the Supreme Lord."
Even for the yogin of supreme bliss, [it is said]: "Such words as 'this muchness' and so forth are far removed; it is to be known through one's own experience.
It is that such radiance in its entirety, which is called the 'pursuit of the discourse of consciousness,'" and so on.
Everything else has been explained in the section titled "The Immaculate Mirror of the Contemplation of the Form of Śiva," and should be looked for there; enough of this digression.
He now further specifies that very sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*) which arises from the vision of the radiant power (*śakti*):
"The ego (*ahaṅkāra*) consists of consciousness (*citta*), its form being the state of essential identity with the clearly manifest letter *A*."
Victorious is the mass of the Śiva-Śakti couple, who has swallowed the entire circle of the worlds! || 5 ||
The meaning of the term *cidvallī* is as follows: *Ahaṅkāra* is that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the form "I, I, I," which manifests the experience of the memory of the emergent Self.
Its *kāra*—that is, its cause—is *ahaṅkāra*. Such an *ahaṅkāra* "conquers," meaning it exists with supreme excellence. Thus it has been said:
The repose of light within itself is declared to be the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva).

It consists of consciousness (*citta*), has knowledge as its sole nature, and possesses the form of a perfectly manifest *ā* and *ha*. *Ā* and *ha* are *ahau*. They are "perfectly manifest" (*suvyaktau*), meaning clearly evident; their forms are mutually emergent, thus they are "perfectly manifest *ā* and *ha*" (*suvyaktāhau*). Their "equal flavor" (*samarasa*) is their becoming one, a single fusion.

The *ākāra* is one's own essential form (*nijarūpa*), which is the light of Śiva (*śivaprakāśa*) and the reflective awareness of Śakti (*śaktivimarśa*). This couple, consisting of this dual form, becomes a single mass (*piṇḍībhavati*), that is, they become unified as one. That wherein this occurs is the "mass-couple of Śiva and Śakti" (*śivaśaktimithunapiṇḍa*). For this very reason, he is one by whom the circle of the worlds (*bhuvanamaṇḍala*)—the aggregate of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*)—has been swallowed (*kavalīkṛta*), meaning it has been internalized and held within.

This is the meaning: by the principle of *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive withdrawal), the expansion of the entire phenomenal world—consisting of both word and meaning—arises precisely from the encapsulation (*sampuṭa*) of light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*), which take the form of the *ahaṃkāra* containing within itself the entire collection of phonemes. Thus says the Śruti: "That one phoneme, through its connection with manifold powers, bestows many phonemes whose meanings are inherent. Also in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad]: "When asked 'Who are you?', he replied, 'I am. It is I alone who am this..."
Everything! Therefore, "I" is the designation for all. In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:

"Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the omnipresent one, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful, the sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, who stands beyond darkness."

Having stated, "He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra, he is the imperishable, supreme, self-ruling Lord," and having declared, "By knowing 'I am that Brahman,' one is liberated from all bonds," [the text] points out that Brahman is the very form of Kāmakāmeśvarī, and thus ordains that her worship is likewise identical with the Self of Brahman. In that same work, elsewhere:

"By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedanta and also the knower of the Vedas. Thus, Brahman is pointed out as being of the very nature of "I. Also in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, after describing the meditation on the form of "I" in the passage, "Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun,'" it states the sublation [of any contrary view] regarding the opposite case: "Then..."

"He who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like a beast," as stated elsewhere in that very same [text]: "Where one thinks, 'I am indeed this all,' like a god or like a king—that is his supreme world. And likewise: "'O venerable deity, I am indeed You; You are indeed I,' and so forth. Similarly, in the Gītā-bhāṣya:

"Those who, having abandoned their own Self, meditate upon another deity, are like those who, having begged for abundant wealth, remain hungry even after begging. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*: "The phoneme of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is threefold sound, consisting of words, mantras, and syllables."
"The meaning of the worlds, kalās, and tattvas is thus the nature of the dharmīs of this Light: 'I am the one whose form is unceasing light, the essence of all splendors and darknesses.
Likewise, 'I'—he is called the One; such is his state of pure subjectivity (ahantā). Also, in the *Rahasyāgama*:
"By means of the state of the full subjectivity (pūrṇāhantā), and not by artificial subjectivity..."
He who perceives the self directly by means of the self—he truly sees.
Beyond this, the Great Bindu enters into that which consists of consciousness by means of two [bindus]; thus, having described the nature of the Bindu, he teaches the Kāmakalā:
"The pair of white and red bindus, which are the distinct Śiva and Śakti whose expansion and contraction [constitute their nature]."
The cause of the creation of both word and meaning is clearly seen as mutually interpenetrating.
The *bindu* is the essence of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the sun is the form of the union of this couple;
Kāma, by virtue of his desirability, and Kalā are the two *bindus* whose forms are fire and moon. (7)

"Cidvallī" means white and bright; "śoṇa" means red. A pair of dots (bindus) having those two colors [is formed]. Therefore, it is that action in which Śiva and Śakti—distinct yet characterized by a mutual tendency to sport—are present. For this very reason, it is "contracting-expanding," meaning the expansion in the form of world-creation is contracting and becoming closed like a bud.

That in which there is expansion; that is, the manifestation of all words and meanings in the forms of *parā*, *paśyantī*, and so forth, consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) from Śiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*).
Their "creation" is the fashioning of the world consisting of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). The cause for this is the causal agent. Thus it is said in the *Saubhāgyahṛdaya*:
"The phoneme (*varṇa*), the energy (*kalā*), the word (*pada*), the principle (*tattva*), the mantra, and likewise the world (*bhuvana*)."
Thus, O Goddess, the six paths shine within you, the conscious self.

"Mutually interpenetrated" means clearly entered into one another, having gone within each other; "distinct" means that which is yet separate. The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: one should contemplate such a pair of white and red drops, the divine couple in the form of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī. Herein lies this supreme secret: according to the method stated in the Śruti, "He who is the Supreme is Maheśvara," He is the progenitor of all words beginning with the Vedas, denoted by the syllable Anuttara (A).

The Supreme Lord, having entered the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*)—which consists of the abode of the entire universe that has become His own self—assumes the state of the *bindu*.

Then, that power of reflective awareness also enters the *bindu* consisting of light (*prakāśa*) which is contained within itself. Thereupon, the *bindu* becomes swollen; from that *bindu*, there emerges the power consisting of sound (*nādātmikā*), which contains all the principles (*tattva*), is composed of splendor, and takes on a form as subtle as the tip of a grain of wild rice (*nīvāra*). Thus, it assumes the nature of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). And so it is said:

The body of those two, which are of the nature of *bindu* and *nāda*, and of *prakāśa* and *vimarśa*, is "I" (*aham*). Thus, between these two forms, one *vimarśa* assumes the form of the red *bindu*, while the other, *prakāśa*, attains the state of the white *bindu*. Through the union of both, there arises the mixed form, consisting of all splendor, which is the essential nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This meaning has been thoroughly determined in the *Rahasyāmnāya*, in the chapter titled *Candracandrikā*, within the dialogue between *Prakāśa* and *Vimarśa*: "I am the white *bindu*, O Goddess, and you are the red *bindu*. By our mutual union, we become the Supreme Self. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* (Mālinīvijayottara), in the chapter on the *Sṛṣṭikrama*, this very point is established: "The *bindu* is the supreme *prakāśa*, and *vimarśa* is the *nāda*. Their union is the *visarga*; that is the supreme reality. And in the *Triśirobhairava*, in the chapter on the *Kulakramasadbhāva*, it is stated: "The *bindu* is the supreme *prakāśa*, and *vimarśa* is the *nāda*. Their union is the *visarga*; that is the supreme reality. Therefore, the essence of the Supreme Self is the union of *prakāśa* and *vimarśa*, which is the *visarga*. This is the ultimate truth.
"Be gracious, O Blessed Śambhu! Whatever doubt I have regarding the worship of the Self, you ought to explain that to me—
[the doubt] concerning the investigation of the Self for one whose form has been made supreme through the contemplation of the Self."
To the Goddess who had asked, "O Blessed One, O Lord, tell me how that which is supreme bliss [is attained]," the Supreme Lord replied:
"That which is the support of all, which stands above everything..."
Having merged one's own self into that Self, one should go to the Supreme. Since the world is the Self of us both, and because of our identity with you,
know that for all who possess knowledge, the worship of the Self is bliss.
Because of their identity and so forth, both the world and the vital breath are indeed unborn for us; having known these [principles] completely, one should correctly know the supreme consciousness.
— Reflection.

Śiva provides the answer to this fivefold set of questions—beginning with "How can there be identity between us two? How can even a union be possible? How can there be equality of karma? And how [can we be] those who are beyond conduct and are *avadhūtas*?"—as follows:
"If you say that the supreme reality beyond Śivakāma is being described, listen, O Dear One: that objection is not capable of being addressed, for it transcends the sphere of speech;
yet when the will of Śiva—known as Pāri—is present, then she becomes *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)."
O Dear One, from the seed-syllable, that which is called *parārṇa* is born like a sprout from a seed.
Once it has entered the power (*śakti*), it becomes condensed by the *vāmā* and other [energies];
rich with the womb of all seeds, it attains the state of the subtle point (*sūkṣmabindu*).
Having entered that, she became Ambikā and attained a state of blissful form;
through her pervasion, she expanded, and from that, the *bindu* reached a state of swelling.
Thus, having burst through the *bindu*, she arose like the tip of a grain of wild rice (*nīvāra*).
Arising simultaneously with [the universe], emulating millions of eternal rays,
richly pregnant with the thirty-six principles, and profound as the primordial syllable, she enters the supreme bindu of the male state and attains the state of resonance (dhvani).
That [bindu] also attains the state of its own power, which is the womb of power consisting of sound (nāda).
Of those two distinct [aspects], one becomes red and the other becomes white; that which is mixed with the central bindu consists of the nature of the void within the bulb (kanda) of the suṣumnā.

By these and other such statements, the description of the three *bindus* has been provided. Here, a few points have been mentioned in this context; everything else must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. The *Śruti* also says: "The one phoneme [becomes manifold] through the application of powers," and so forth. This very same description of the three *bindus* is further elucidated by the statement: "The *bindu* is the self of *ahaṅkāra*. The *bindu* is of the nature already described. *Ahaṅkāra* is the identity with the letter *ha*, which is the expansion of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and the form of the letter *ā*, wherein the entire collection of phonemes is internally contained.

He whose nature is that [nature]. By the rule *varṇāt kāraḥ*, the suffix *kāra* is added to the word *ahaṃ*, just as in the case of *ekāra*. Therefore, he has the form of the "equal flavor" (*samarasa*) of this couple; that is, of the couple consisting of Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*), which are expressed by the letters *a* and *ha* respectively.
"Couple" (*mithuna*) means a pair; specifically, a couple in the form of divine husband and wife. "Equal flavor" (*samarasa*) refers to their mutual conformity as they penetrate one another.
He whose very form (*ākāra*) is that [very essence] is such a Sun (*ravi*). This means a mixed drop (*miśrabindu*), having become a single flavor (*samarasībhūta*) of white and red drops.
Even in the world, one describes the Sun as having a mixed nature based on the scriptural accounts of the entry and exit of Agni and Soma:
"In this way, either fire ascends after the rising sun, or the sun enters the fire at evening."

From scripture: because the etymology of the word *amā*—that "the sun and moon (*sūryācandramasau*) stay together (*saha*) on this lunar day (*tithi*)"—is well-known to refer to the entry and exit of the moon and the sun, therefore the mixed point (*miśrabindu*) itself is the sun. For this very reason, [the text] states its status as an object of worship: "Desire" (*kāma*).
It is called "desire" because it is desired—that is, longed for as one's own self by great yogins who know the ultimate reality. The reason for this is "by way of being desirable."
This is its loveliness. Thus it is said in the Upaniṣad: "With a golden beard and golden hair, he is entirely golden down to his very nails.
And in the Īśāvāsya as well:
"He has pervaded all, He who is radiant, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, and untouched by evil."

Likewise, in that very same [text]: "I behold that most auspicious form of yours; that which is the Supreme Person, that am I. Having thus addressed the exceedingly beautiful Lord of Desire, it reflects upon His such majesty. In the Rahasyāmnāya:
"The unsurpassed, the supportless, the ocean of Being-Consciousness-Bliss."
"That which is this Śāmbhava [state], having attained the status of the substratum of liberation," and so forth.

*Kalā* is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*). *Dahana* is fire; *indu* is the moon. Those two, whose forms (*vigraha*) are the shapes of the *bindu* and the moon, are the *bindus* whose forms are fire and moon. The meaning is this: the power of reflective awareness has the nature of Agni and Soma. She is inseparable from Kāmeśvara, who is the manifestation of both of them.
Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is the totality of the *bindu*, is called Kāmakalā; she alone is proclaimed in all the *Āgamas* as the object of worship. For it is said:
"Śiva, who is white, [unites] with Śakti, who is red, through the piercing of Parā-Śāmbhavī."
By means of the supreme principle (parātattva) in the form of the red Śambhu, through Śakti.
"Śiva is red within the white Śakti due to the state of oneness with the Supreme Śambhu;
Śiva is red within the white Śakti, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere:
I bow to your supreme digit, O Supreme Śivā, whose face is fashioned from the foremost *bindu*, whose pair of breasts is formed by other *bindus*,
and who is the locus for the thread of the *nāda-bindu*.

One should eternally worship this Supreme Goddess, whose face is the sun-dot, whose breasts are the pair of moon and fire-dots shining below it, and whose girdle is the place of the digits of the half-parārdha.

"The *bindu* situated above the vowel *ī* is the mouth; the sun (*bhānu*) situated below are the two breasts; fire and the moon are the two breasts; and the *ardhakalā* is the womb. This is the secret. Herein is the essential summary: [She] consists of the great mantra composed of the infinite mass of phonemes contained within herself; she consists of the full *ahaṃtā*; her essence is light and bliss.

The Great Tripurasundarī, known as Kāmakalā, who consists of the form of the divine syllable that is the synthesis of the three *bindus*, is to be meditated upon incessantly by the supreme yogis of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*) and the great Maheśvaras.
Such majesty is also set forth in the *Brahmopaniṣad*, as follows: "Now, this Person has four stations..."
[These] exist: the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head. Therein, the four-footed Brahman shines forth. In the waking state it is Brahmā;

in the dream state, Viṣṇu; in deep sleep, Rudra. The fourth is the Imperishable (akṣara). It is the Sun, Viṣṇu, and the Lord (Īśvara). It is itself without mind, without ears, without hands or feet, known as light.

The meaning of this is as follows: "The serene joy (*samprasāda*) of this very deity is the bird that moves within" (*antaryāmikhaga*), and so forth. For that Person (*puruṣa*), whose nature has been determined by the preceding network of statements, there are four stations consisting of the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, the region of the throat, and the head.
In these four stations, Brahman—which is all-pervasive, pure, and of transparent luminosity—is four-footed, having twenty-four quarters.
By the etymological derivation that "the Imperishable (*akṣara*) does not perish," it shines forth as the fundamental cause because it is the cause of the origin of the universe.
Regarding this, it is said: "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
Thus, the meaning is that Being, consisting of limitless splendor, radiates. Through instruction regarding the locations and regions of such an Imperishable, [it is revealed].

Having explained the nature of the individual parts (*avayava*), he now explains the fourth, which is the collective form (*samudāyarūpa*), consisting of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), the point (*bindu*), located at the *dvādaśānta*, having the nature of the *kāmakalā*, and composed of supreme light—thus he says: "The fourth is the imperishable (*akṣara*). From the words "He is the Sun" up to "He is the Lord, the waking state," this is the internal [explanation]. The Sun is of the nature of light; Viṣṇu is characterized by pervasion (*vyāpana*); Prāṇa is the individual soul (*jīva*), the giver of life to all; Puruṣa is that in whom everything lives, the living being whose form consists of prāṇa and the rest.
Agni is the leader. The Lord of such a one is Paramaśiva, joined with Kāmeśvarī, who is known as Vimarśa; this is the meaning. And so it is said in the *Atharvaśiras*:

"Now, for what reason is he called Īśāna? Having asked this, it explains itself: "He who rules over all existents by means of his ruling powers, the supreme energies. Likewise elsewhere: "His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed; knowledge, strength, and action are innate to him."

And thus: "Such is Kāmeśvara, whose form consists of the fourth vowel (the letter *AU*). 'Jāgatī' means 'awake' (*jāgratī*); this is because the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85) permits the interchange of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and nominal suffixes (*suP*). Here, 'awakening' refers to that which consists of the *mātṛkā-cakra* composed of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, within the abode of the limitless circle of light called Sarvānandamaya, which constitutes the first middle [layer] of the Śrīcakra."
Established upon the fire of the *bindu*, a mass of consciousness like the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvarta*),
seated comfortably on the lap of Kāmeśvara, she is exceedingly beautiful.

In the manner thus described, [the Lord] possesses the nature of Prakāśānandanātha. With this intention, the term "awake" (*jāgarūka*) is explained by the phrase "intent upon the play of divine sport" (*līlāvinodanodyukta*). He describes that such a syllable as consisting of light (*jyotirmaya*) and partless (*niṣkala*) with the words "among them," and so forth.

Among those syllables whose constituent parts are fashioned through meditation upon specific locations—namely the regions of the foundation (*ādhāra*), the heart, the throat, and the head—that which is supreme...

The imperishable Brahman, which is the fourth state and is called Nirvāṇa, shines forth; it manifests. He describes it as being thus without parts (niṣkala) by means of the words "without shadow," "without wind," and so forth.

He defines the imperishable supreme primordial nature (paramaprakṛti) with the words "known as light" (jyotirviditam). By the words "I bow to the unsurpassed light" and so forth, because its very essence is illumination, it is luminous;
"known" means it is known by all the Vedāntas. Furthermore, the imperishable Brahman, consisting of light, is the self of all.

The Śruti itself clearly declares that the Lord of All is the very nature of Nirvāṇa. For instance, having pointed out Brahman as the Self of all in the passage: "Where there are no worlds, no gods, no Vedas, no sacrifices, no mother, no father, no daughter-in-law, no outcaste (Caṇḍāla), no Pulkasa, no ascetic (Śramaṇa), and no forest-dweller (Tāpasa)—there shines the one alone, the Supreme Brahman," it begins with the words: "That knowledge is in the space within the heart... and so forth.

Having thus described the nature of worship with the words, "That All-pervading One knows through meditation on the creatures," he speaks again: "That supreme Brahman shines forth; it is Nirvāṇa; there the gods, the seers, and the ancestors have no mastery; it is to be realized through all-knowledge. And elsewhere: "It is to be seen by those of subtle vision with another, subtle intellect"—through such scriptural passages, that Imperishable (akṣara) is correctly understood by those who know the ultimate reality.
Likewise, in the *Catuḥśatī*, in the section of twelve verses:
"This triple world, from the cosmic egg down to the shell of the universe, is strung upon the Great Sūtra of the Imperishable; even today, this world is seen [as such]."
Since the three worlds are adorned by the moonlight of its syllables,
a person may strive for perfection through even a single syllable of it.
"I salute that imperishable one, whose form consists of the letters of the alphabet, who is [worshipped] by Ravi, Tārkṣya, Indu, Kandarpa, Śaṅkara, Anala, and Viṣṇu. And in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"But Śiva is always internal bliss, overflowing with the flood of all principles; he is the mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme imperishable.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"One's own self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings; I am the very nature of consciousness, expanded by the undivided awareness of 'I am I.
Thus [it is said]. As in the *Svacchanda-tantra*, beginning with: "Above that, the state beyond mind (*unmanā*) is remembered..."
Here there is no time, no division of time, no unity, and no deity;
that which is called the face of Rudra is the supreme, pure, and perfect nirvāṇa.
O lady of excellent hips, behold that which is known as Śiva-Śakti— free from conceptual construction, stainless, transcendent, wondrous, and beyond both speech and mind.
"Partless and yet with parts, formless and free from conceptual construction, beyond dualities, the supreme reality known as Śiva, the highest state. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, in the *Vijñānabhairava-bhaṭṭāraka*, regarding the wheel (*cakra*) in the form of the *bindu*, according to the sequence of gross phonemes, it extends to the half-moon (*ardhendu*), the *bindu*, and the end of sound (*nādānta*).
"From the utterance of the Void (Śūnya), one becomes Śivā," and so forth. And Amṛtānandayogin says:
"In the supreme space of the Bindu, characterized by Being, Consciousness, and Bliss;
free from phenomenal expansion, without appearance, beyond conceptual construction, and untainted."
In the unsurpassed great void, purified by the realization of the supreme wonder,
which transcends the void and is victorious over the end of all voids;
"In that which is not conceptualized by the designations of female, male, or neuter; which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; which is illumined by the five categories of existence;
which is free from all points of comparison; and whose nature is the experience of luminosity. Thus [it is said].
Śivānandasvāmin also says:

"O Tripurasundarī, who consists of the energies of the Kāmarāja-mantra, whose form is that of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, and who resides within the heart as the totality (sakala) and so forth— salutations to you!"
We too, within the latent impression of consciousness-bliss— pervading the fourfold state from earth up to Śiva, the universal form adorned with the great jewels of the four cosmic eggs— abide.
Having meditated upon the *piṇḍa*, one should contemplate within it the Supreme, which transcends all,
the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītā*), the unsurpassed essence of the nectar of consciousness-bliss.
Even there, one should assume by one's own will the supreme state of waking and so forth,
which consists in the inward-facing repose of all cognitions.

I worship her who resembles infinite millions of moons and suns, who is augmented by sixteen [energies], in whom the collection of the thirty-six principles has attained oneness within herself, who transcends all, and whose form is the Great Bindu.
This and other such passages from the network of Śruti and Smṛti should be investigated. || 6-7 ||
Having thus taught the nature of the Bindu, he states that the fruit of knowing and worshipping it is indeed the state of the Supreme Brahman:
"This is the Kāmakalā-vidyā, whose essence is the Devīcakra.
He by whom this is known becomes liberated, taking the form of Mahātripurasundarī. (8)

The *Kāmakalā*, the Great Tripurasundarī, has been explained by means of the aforementioned great treatise, the *Cidvallī*. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of *vidyā*—that is, knowledge—she possesses, it is said: she consists of the sequence of the goddess’s *cakra*; that is, the *śrīcakra* of the goddess Tripurasundarī. Of that...

The *krama* consists of the wheel, the mantra, and the deity, whose nature encompasses everything from the *sarvānandamaya* up to the final manifest form (*samastaprakaṭa*). That [realization] has that as its essence and takes that as its object.

By means of which it is known by a fortunate and learned person who, through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), desires to know Brahman as it unfolds; having understood it through such means as approaching a guru, that person becomes liberated. According to the position of the *Pratyabhijñā*: "Even here, he for whom sovereignty is made known by the [inner] sciences (*vidyās*) is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) and is indeed liberated."

The supreme yogi dwells having swallowed all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) through the incessant cultivation of the perfect sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), which is highly effective in eradicating the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra. Thus, it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "When men think that by the knowledge of Brahman they shall become everything, what indeed could be unknown to them? That becomes everything. In the end, he becomes the form of Mahātripurasundarī, whose essence is the Supreme Goddess Parābhaṭṭārikā.
It is so; and thus says the Śruti: "They enter the supreme abode, the Tripura. And: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
Seeing thus, thinking thus, knowing thus, he becomes one whose delight is the Self, whose play is the Self, whose companion is the Self, whose bliss is the Self—he indeed becomes that.

And likewise in the Pratyabhijñā-sūtra: "By virtue of the full sense of 'I' (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva), which consists of the Mantra and Vidyā whose essence is Light and Bliss, [the yogi] becomes the master of the dissolution of all things."
"The attainment of the state of the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvaratā) occurs through one's own consciousness as the deity. Thus [ends the section on] Śiva. And Abhinavaguptapāda says:

"He in whom this [reality], manifested in the form of the sequence for the sake of others, shines forth—he, whose nature is consciousness and the bliss of the non-sequential, is Maheśvara by virtue of his supreme joy."
"Independent, the sovereign of the wheels of consciousness, the Great Lord,
served by the wheel of the deities of awareness— may that certain one be victorious!
Thus it is said in the *Svacchanda-śāstra*.
But when he is firmly established in one [state], then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, he attains the status of the enjoyer; from that, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara).

Hundreds of such statements are to be observed. And by the passage beginning, "He by whom this is thus known is liberated," it is stated that only practice preceded by knowledge leads to the attainment of Brahman. Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "O Gārgī, he who, without knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years—all that becomes for him merely finite. And so too in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"As long as one does not know these three supreme conventions, so long will one not become a bearer of the supreme command within the wheel of Tripurā.
Therefore, it is only through practice preceded by knowledge that one becomes Paramaśiva. And it is said in that very same place: "Without knowing this, O fair-hipped one..."

"One shall immediately attain the state of moving through the sky. Enough of this digression following upon a digression. I carry this *Kāmakalā*, which bestows bliss and has arisen from the moon-like face of Puṇyānanda, perpetually upon my head, with my speech, and in my heart.

Thus, this commentary on the *Kāmakalā*, titled *Cidvallī*, has been composed by Naṭanānanda for the pleasure of his teacher and for the contemplation of men who are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*). Among them, he—one of their number—composed this commentary out of devotion to him. Although many commentaries on this *Kāmakalā* have been cited by predecessors, nevertheless, Naṭanānanda has also contemplated it with devotion. The great-souled Puṇyānanda, having thus released the drop (*bindu*) that is the form of the *Kāmakalā*— [End of fragment]

Devoted to Sundarī, he now endeavors to describe the Śrīcakra, which is the form of the unfolding of the Bindu; and by the grace of the feet of his Guru alone, he also begins to explain the *Śrīkāmakalāvilāsa*, which is a commentary on its sequence. (8)

In this context, the Great Maheśvaras, who are blissful through merit, having experienced the beautiful Sundarī known as Kāmakalā as their own primordial self, and being further intent upon the experience of the play consisting of the deities of the mantra-cakra,

begin to describe the origination of the universe and so forth from the very Mahābindu, which is the fundamental reality: "From the blossomed, reddish Bindu, the sound— the sprout of the Brahman of Nāda— became manifest."
Therefore, there is the production of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and color. || 9 ||
Now, even from a subtle drop arises the birth of ether, air, fire, water, and earth;
this world, from the atom up to the cosmic egg, is a transformation of these five elements.

"From the red drop (*bindu*) that has burst forth from the *cidvallī* (the creeper of consciousness)"—that is, from the swollen [drop]. From the *bindu* possessing the characteristics previously described, there arises the sprout of *nāda-brahman*.
*Nāda* is the phoneme that is the cause of the production of all sounds. That itself is *brahman*; it is the sprout of that *brahman*, meaning that which has it as its producer. Thus:
And it has been said:
"The single phoneme whose essence is sound (nāda) possesses all divisions of sound;
because its nature never sets, it is called 'unstruck' (anāhata). Thus.

The *Upaniṣad* also states: "The meditator, Rudra, having established the vital breath along with the senses in the Supreme Self at the end of the *nāda*, meditates upon the Lord. And *Dīpikānanda* says: "The *vyāma*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*—such is the sound (*rava*), the word (*śabda*), which is the sprout of the *nāda-brahman*, appearing in the form of *paśyantī* and so forth; it has become manifest (*vyakta*), i.e., arisen.
