Later, in the passage beginning with 'the form of the internal ascent' (*antaroharūpā*) and so on, [it is described] as the powers of the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), such as *parā*, *paśyantī*, and the rest."

Because it is taught [thus]: from that sound (śabda), the origin—that is, the production—of the five elements (bhūtas), namely ether, air, fire, water, and earth, as well as the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', is declared. This is the meaning: it is traditionally taught that the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) arises from that very Nāda-Bindu.
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman is of the nature of sound (śabdātmaka).

Objection: Is it not the case that from such passages as "From the Self, space was produced," the origin of the world from space—which is itself [derived] from the Self—is heard in scripture? How then can it be said that [the world arises] from the Śabdabrahman consisting of *bindu* and *nāda* alone? Reply: It is said—in all the Vedāntas, we observe the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world, consisting of words such as Parā, Paśyantī, and so forth, precisely from the syllable of knowledge (*vidyākṣara*) which consists of *bindu* and *nāda*. And thus says the Śruti: "From the Imperishable, here in this world, it is born..."

"The universe—that imperishable which the creators of beings and all the gods worship. Also in another Upaniṣad: "In the divine city of Brahman, the stainless, partless, pure, and imperishable shines forth.

This means that the nature of the syllable *kāmakalā*—which is the aggregate of the three *bindus* and is devoid of the letters *ka* and *la* contained within the *kāmarāja-bīja*—shines forth. Having described its luminous nature (*jyotirmayatva*), it is stated that even beyond the state of insentience, that Supreme Brahman shines forth; thus [the text speaks] of the imperishable Brahman which is the primary subject.

Having described the nature of light and taught its essential form, he concludes by stating that Brahman is indeed of the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara), as declared at the beginning of the *Upāsanā-upaniṣad* through the resting of the *nirvāṇabindu* within the *miśrabindu*. With this very meaning in mind, the *Laghubhaṭṭārikā* also says:
"That which is your eternal, partless (*niṣkala*) syllable of the mantra, [known as] Kāmarāja."

Thus, in this verse, they declared that the syllable *kāmakalā*, being the root of all the Vedas, is desirable to all persons in every respect and bestows liberation. Its commentators, the venerable Kṛṣṇānanda Varya, likewise established the majesty of the very nature of the syllable *śrīkāmakalā* by citing a collection of scriptural passages such as, "If one hears it, he hears what is not heard; indeed, he does not know the path of merit. The ancients as well—
The poets [state]: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the Word known as the Imperishable;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds. Thus.

They declare that the origin of the universe proceeds from the Imperishable Brahman (*akṣarabrahman*) itself. Likewise: "In this world, she who is the mother of all sounds is called Vāgvādinī. Thus she is of the nature of nectar. Smṛti also states:
"The Goddess Tripurasundarī consists of the Śabdabrahman and is translucent."

Thus is the manifestation of sound (*śabda*); [it is said that] "the moving and the unmoving are pervaded by sound," and so forth. Likewise, in the passage "from the Self, space [is born]," there is no dispute that the word *ātman* refers to the Imperishable Self (*akṣarātman*). Having thus stated that the Red Bindu (*śoṇabindu*) is the self of all and the creator of all, he extends this same nature to the White Bindu (*śubhrabindu*) as well through non-difference from it, beginning with the words "Now, from the Clear" (*atha viśadāt*): "From the Clear" means from that which illuminates everything; "from the Bindu" refers to the Bindu previously explained; [and from] the infinite [Bindu] consisting of the five elements beginning with space (*gagana*).
The meaning is that the manifestation and dissolution of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) occur. And so says the Śruti:
"In which all beings are dissolved, and having been dissolved, they attain manifestation;
and again, becoming unmanifest, they are born once more like bubbles."
From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses;
as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which sustains the universe.
Thus it is established that everything is created from Brahman, which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), composed of red and white drops (*bindu*).
Like the spreading canopy of rays of the universe manifested by its own will, I bow to the Great Seat of Consciousness (*saṃvin-mahāpīṭha*), which is the locus of the feet of Śiva and Śakti. (9–10)

Having thus explained the non-duality of the two points (*bindu*), he speaks of the identity between the mantra and the deity as well: "Just as the two points are devoid of mutual difference, so too there is not even a trace of difference between the Vidyā and the Deity, who are the object of knowledge and the knower. (11)

The *cidvallī* consists of two *bindus*, which are of the nature of the previously mentioned *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Just as— in the manner described by the statement, "The wise say that the single reality is 'Śiva-Śakti,' for they are inseparable"— they are mutually embraced, in that very same manner [it is so] with the *vidyā* and the deity.

The Vidyā consists of fifteen syllables; the Deity is Mahātripurasundarī. Between these two—the object of knowledge and the knower, or the signified and the signifier—there is not even a trace of difference, nor even the slightest distinction. Nevertheless, in the Sāṅkhyāyana Śākhā belonging to the Ṛgveda, it is said:
"Kāma, Yoni, Kamalā, Vajrapāṇi, Guhā, Ha, Sā, Mātariśvan, Abhra, and Indra."
Furthermore, this Guhā, who is the mother of the universe and the primordial Vidyā, is manifold through her entire illusory power (māyā).

Having extracted the two vidyās beginning with *ka* and *ha* by means of the passage starting with, "The sixth, then the seventh, and the one whose charioteer is fire; in this [vidyā], they teach the triad beginning with *mūla*," he states their identity of deity with the words, "the Viśvamātṛ-vidyā and so forth. Also in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: "This person who is in the right eye—his head is *bhūḥ*.
'One head,' and this single syllable is *bhuvaḥ*. The two arms—two arms, these two syllables are *svaḥ*, the two feet."

"These two syllables are its two supports; its secret name (*upaniṣad*) is 'I' (*aham*). "He who knows thus slays evil and casts it off. Having pointed out the constituent parts beginning with *bhūḥ* belonging to the Person residing in the eye, and having taught that the state of this imperishable one is the nature of Brahman as the "I," [the text] declares his sovereignty preceded by the cessation of all sins. And therefore, of all sciences...

There is no dispute on this point: that because [the Self] consists of the *mātṛkā*—which is of the nature of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) and the cause for the manifestation of all sounds such as those at the beginning of the Vedas—there is non-difference between the two.
Thus, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*: "O Dear One, all mantras consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), and they, in turn, consist of power (*śakti*)."
Power (śakti) should be known as Mātṛkā, and she should be known as having Śiva as her essence.
"That Mātṛkā who exists in the world, endowed with supreme splendor— by her all this is pervaded, from the realm of Brahmā down to the self.
Thus, that which is perceived, that which is known, and even the object of cognition, becomes nothing other than consisting of consciousness itself.
Does wood not become fire when it is offered as an oblation into the fire?

Krodhabhaṭṭāraka also, having stated, "Born from the fifty syllables arising from one's own body," and so forth, declared the identity of the mantra and the deity with the words, "O Mātṛkā, pervading the universe with your own self, you manifest as 'I am, I am'. Thus, the meaning of the verse is complete. || 11 ||
To explain that the entire universe manifests from this inseparable couple of Sound (nāda) and Bindu, he says that this very couple, through its own will, brought about its own differentiation:
"Word and meaning are eternally united with one another; these two consist of Śakti and Śiva."
The distinctions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution are divided threefold by way of the three seed-syllables.

The meaning of the term *cidvallī* is as follows: "Speech and its object" (*vāgarthau*). Speech consists of phonemes, words, and mantras; the object consists of the *kalās*, *tattvas*, and worlds (*bhuvanas*).

For this very reason, they take that form, because it is heard in scripture that the entire expansion of the universe, consisting of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), arises precisely from word and object, which are of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Thus, in the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*: "The spark of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is threefold sound, consisting of words, mantras, and phonemes;
such is the attribute of Light. For this very reason, they are eternally conjoined and inseparably united;
for their connection is not occasional, like that between a jar and a cloth, since if that were the case, all logical consistency would be undermined.

The distinction between creation, maintenance, and dissolution: creation (*sṛṣṭi*) is the manifestation of the network of principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth; maintenance (*sthiti*) is their preservation;

dissolution (*laya*) is the direct realization of them as one's own self. These are the two [powers] characterized by such a distinction, due to the differentiation of those three which have arisen from one's own self. Thus says Abhinavagupta: "He exists as having the nature of creation and withdrawal through his own self."

Mutually, they consist of Śakti and Śiva, whose essential nature is *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). Because these two are one, like fire and its burning power, there is no separate reality (*tattvāntara*) between them; this is the meaning. Thus, scripture states: "Because we two are the self of the universe, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between us as well," and so forth. And the statement of the learned is: "The identity of these two is established, like that of fire and its burning power. These aforementioned *prakāśa* and *vimarśa* are threefold, in three ways.
To the question "By what means are they differentiated?", he says: "in the form of the three seeds"—meaning, consisting of the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti.

This is the meaning: Mahātripurasundarī, whose form is the syllable Kāmakalā which is the aggregate of the three points (bindus), and who consists of the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava, is the object of worship for all. Thus it is said in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
Vāgīśvarī, whose nature consists of the three powers of the phonemes taught in the three principles,
is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the source of speech (vāgbhava), and the embodiment of liberation.

She is the passion for desire, the art of desire, whose nature consists of the activity of the form of desire; she is the Supreme Power within the seed-syllable of Śakti, who is indeed Will in the form of Knowledge.
"Thus the Goddess, whose self consists of three syllables, the Great Tripurasundarī,
when known through the lineage tradition, is the liberator from the bonds of worldly existence.
Following this, he begins to extract the venerable fifteen-syllabled Vidyā by means of describing the specific subjects contained within the three sections beginning with the *Vāgbhava*.
The Mother (mātṛkā), the measure (māna), and the measurable (meya) are the forms of the seed-syllables divided by the three points (bindu);
they are also conceived through the distinctions of the three abodes (dhāman), the three seats (pīṭha), and the three powers (śakti). || 13 ||
Within them, there are respectively the three genders and likewise the three Mātṛkās.
Thus, this triple city is the Vidyā that distinguishes the fourth seat and the rest.

The mother is *cidvallī*, the knower is Maheśvara, the means of knowledge (*māna*) is the *vidyā* which serves as the instrument for that realization, and the object of knowledge (*meya*) is Mahātripurasundarī as she is being known. These three—the knower, the knowledge, and the known—are the forms of the three seeds differentiated by the three *bindus*. The "three *bindus*" refers to the triad of the *bindus* mentioned previously.

That which is of a mixed red-and-white form is distinct from and separate from that [supreme] Self; it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) known as *nirvāṇa*, which constitutes the totality of all things. Its forms are the manifestors of that [seed]. The meaning is this: the Supreme Light itself—which consists of the experience of the Self as a mass of consciousness and bliss transcending all—sports while assuming the states of the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyabhāva*), characterized by the sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*).

Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. Having reflected, He saw nothing other than Himself. He first uttered, 'I am. Thereupon, He became known by the name 'I. Therefore even now, when addressed, one first says, 'It is I,' and then utters another name.

The meaning of this is as follows: "The Self" refers to the Supreme Lord alone. "In the beginning, this" refers to the manifest universe; the sense is that [the Self] existed with the phenomenal world contained within Himself.

Thus, that Supreme Self, having investigated and perceived the universe as being identical with His own self, saw nothing else whatsoever apart from Himself; for He had swallowed everything within Himself. At that time, manifesting before creation—prior to all things—the unique form corresponding to His own nature as the solid mass of indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss, He declared, "I am," thereby displaying His identity. From that very moment, the name "Aham" (I) came into existence.

This is because Brahman alone reveals its own true nature. Indeed, "I" (aham) is the very name of Brahman. Therefore, even in this verse, when one is addressed by someone asking "Who are you?", having first stated the nature of Brahman as "I," one subsequently mentions other names and so forth.

Consequently, the meaning is that in all cases, through the perception of one's own true nature, it is Brahman alone that is established as the knower and so on, appearing in various differentiated forms. As it is said in the *Catuḥśatī*:
But that supreme past radiance consists of the arising of one's own self-awareness;
it is the universal form, inlaid with the delineations of the universe as manifested by its own will.
Consciousness is the nature of the Self, beautiful with innate bliss;
yet its radiance contracts through the expansions of the object, the subject, the act of knowing, and the means of knowledge.
Also in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"We bow to that Śiva who, though his own nature is undivided, [appears] as a manifold conceptualization of subjects within the wheel of the maṇḍala of his own heart."

The "three abodes" (*dhāmatraya*) refers to the three spheres of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; the "three seeds" (*bījatraya*) are those beginning with *Vāgbhava*; the "three seats" (*pīṭhatraya*) are Kāmagiri and the others; and the "three powers" (*śaktitraya*) are Will and the rest. Contemplated through such divisions as these, because they consist of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*), within these threefold-distinct abodes and so forth, there exists in due order the triad of *liṅgas*—beginning with the *Svayambhū*—and the triad of *mātṛkās*—distinguished by the divisions of *Akatha* and the rest. She is the totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpā*) because she fulfills all such entities.

He states that the supreme power named Tripurā has manifested: "In this way, she whose cities are threefold... In this manner, by the previously mentioned method, she is she whose *purīs*—that is, bodies—are three in number. For this very reason, she is the Fourth Seat (*turīyapīṭha*), meaning she is the ground for the manifestation and withdrawal of the entire universe consisting of the threefold nature.
Thus it has been said: "The Mātṛkā in the form of the Seat," and also in the *Svacchanda-tantra*: "And she is manifested in the Svacchanda."

And in the Subālopaniṣad it is said: "One enters only into bliss; one rises up and attains only the Fourth (turiya). That which is the Fourth—this indeed is the immortal, fearless, sorrowless, infinite, and seedless [state] into which one enters," so he spoke. Such is she who, though non-different from the Fourth Seat and the like, manifests by her own will within her own self as a multitude of infinite principles; she whose essence is indivisible consciousness.
And thus it has been said:

"Because she appeared before the three emanations (*trimūrti*), because she exists prior [to them], because she consists of the triple Veda (*trayīmaya*), and because she fills the three worlds, the name of the Mother (*Ambikā*) is generally 'Tripurā'.

Thus, "the Goddess Tripurā is one's own consciousness (*svasaṃvit*). Her essential nature is woven together by all the principles (*tattva*) manifested through her sovereignty; she is composed of the primordial Fire, Sun, and Moon...
"By means of the abodes of the [reflected] images," and so forth. Hereafter, from that [source], there arises the manifestation of the colors of space, wind, fire, water, and earth. (13–14)

He begins to describe the nature of the deity, which consists of great mantras characterized by specific syllable counts, based upon the five elements created at the beginning and expressed through the description of their qualities:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*).
The first is the pervader, while the latter is the pervaded; thus, in sequence, there are fifteen.
This Nityā, who consists of fifteen syllables, is indeed considered to be material;
likewise, the eternal qualities such as sound, which are divided into various distinctions, are pervaded by her.
The lunar days (tithis) are eternal and take the form of the lunar phases; they are the embodiment of the perfect union of Śiva and Śakti.
They consist of day and night, and those venerable phonemes (varṇas) likewise possess the nature of that same duality.

The meaning of the term *cidvallī* is as follows: sound is the quality of space (*ākāśa*); touch is the quality of air (*vāyu*); form is the quality of fire (*tejas*); taste is the quality of water (*vāri*); and smell is the quality of earth (*pṛthivī*).
These qualities, beginning from space and ending with earth, result in fifteen qualities through the successive addition of one quality at each stage.
Through the fifteen-fold nature of these qualities, the Śrīvidyā has become fifteen-syllabled. He states that she has manifested as having that very nature: "in the form of fifteen syllables.

She is considered and desired (*abhimatā*) as being related to the elements (*bhautikāmitā*). For this very reason, she takes the form of fifteen syllables, because the qualities manifested from her own self consist of fifteen aspects. Thus, the syllables of the Vidyā are also fifteen. Having that form, having that nature, she is eternal, immutable, and like a wave.

The meaning is that it is the ground for the manifestation of all principles (tattvas), like an ocean for bubbles and foam. Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "This great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of pure consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, returns and merges back into them. And in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "In which all states of being dissolve. And Śivānanda says:
"The collection of thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth."
I bow to that great ocean of consciousness, in which there is no existence of waves or bubbles.

Thus, it is said that the sixteenth [digit], which is indeed immutable (*kūṭasthā*), assumes the form of the fifteen-syllabled mantra consisting of the fifteen deities, established upon the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) composed of fifteen parts: "The Nityās have the form of the lunar days. The "Nityās" are those beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā. They are "of the form of the lunar days," meaning they are the deities presiding over the lunar days. And the lunar days are those beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon (*pūrṇimā*). They are of the nature of the union (*samarasa*) of Śiva and Śakti.

They possess the form of the union (*sampuṭa*) of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). For this very reason, they consist of day and night, having the nature of day and night, because *prakāśa* and *vimarśa* are composed of day and night. As it has been said in the *Cidvilāsa*: "Night is that which deludes all the world, while day is indeed that which awakens everything. These lunar days (*tithis*) are the venerable phonemes (*śrī-varṇāḥ*). They too, in the manner previously described, take fifteen forms. The venerable phonemes are contained within the *vidyā*.

The groups of phonemes (*varṇagaṇāḥ*) are exceedingly absorbed in that [Essence], meaning they consist of such light and awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*). This fifteen-syllable mantra is recorded in the *Sāṅkhyāyana* recension of the *Ṛgveda*, beginning with: "Kāma is the womb, Kamalā... and so forth. Some describe how this very knowledge (*vidyā*) shines forth elsewhere in that same Veda, in passages such as: "Four [priests] support Him; they bestow security... and so on.

This is the distinction here: this very Supreme Power (parā-śakti), consisting of light (prakāśa) and awareness (vimarśa), composed of the five elements, has become the embodiment of the deities presiding over the lunar days (tithis) corresponding to fifteen mantra-syllables, through the process of the progressive increase of qualities. Thus, according to the scripture: "The one and only Supreme Maheśvara, known as Light (prakāśa), is an ineffable something."
That which is called Śakti and Vimarśa is eternally extolled by the wise.
And that Goddess, known as Vimarśa, has attained a fivefold state through the division of ether,
wind, fire, water, and earth.
By the gradual increase of each individual quality, she has attained the number of lunar days (tithis);
she is the eternal Goddess known as the Sixteenth (Ṣoḍaśī), whose nature is that of reflective discernment (vimarśa).
That Supreme Goddess Tripurā has proceeded through sixteen divisions, beginning with Sundarī and the others, ending with Vicitrā, all around.

This should be understood from the *Āgama* itself by means of mere symbolic terminology (*saṅketa*). O Dear One, he who worships each one of these goddesses, starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), shall attain good fortune.

Also, in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*: "I worship the pervasive [energies]—space, air, fire, water, and earth—which pervade the ten and five [elements] according to the distinctions of their qualities, such as sound and the rest. (15–17)

Beyond this, there is not even a trace of difference between Vidyā and the Deity, as they are both the object of knowledge and the knower; thus, in order to reinforce the point already stated, he clearly declares that Vidyā— just like the Deity— is both immanent in the universe and transcendent of it, her form being manifested through the divisions of the vowels, consonants, and the three Bindus taken collectively.
Vidyā consists of the thirty-six principles, and it is also that which transcends the principles, being absolute. || 18 ||
The Vidyā as well is of such a nature—that subtle Goddess Tripurasundarī;
the Noble Ones maintain the absolute non-difference between the Vidyā and that which is to be known by the Vidyā. || 19 ||

In the term *cidvallī* ("the creeper of consciousness"), *acaḥ* refers to the vowels (*svarāḥ*), and *vyañjanāni* refers to the consonants (*hal̥aḥ*). The *bindutrayam* refers to the three *anusvāras*.

Their *samaṣṭiḥ* is their collective state as a whole; *bhedaḥ* is their state as individual parts. Having these as their manifested form—that is, having their essential nature revealed—it is therefore the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattvātmā*). It is the Self.

She whose form consists of the principles from the earth up to speech (*vāk*), yet who transcends the principles; she who has crossed beyond them because she is the locus for the entire collection and assembly of the principles;
for this very reason, she is *kevalā* (absolute), being alone since there is nothing distinct from her. Such is the meaning of the venerable fifteen-syllabled Vidyā.
This is the method here for the division of the constituent parts of the Vidyā. In this regard, the Puṇyānandas are those who possess the utmost devotion to the *Hādi-vidyā*.

Relying on the state of being a collection of parts within this very Vidyā, they declare its nature to consist of both the principles (tattvas) and that which transcends them. Here, in the first section called Vāgbhava, there are five vowels and seven consonants, totaling twelve syllables. In the second section called Kāmarāja, there are six vowels and eight consonants, totaling fourteen syllables. In the third section called Śakti, there are four vowels and six consonants, totaling ten syllables.

There are ten vowels; all together, they comprise thirty-six syllables. However, some maintain that there are six vowels and six consonants in the first section, seven vowels and seven consonants in the second section, and five vowels and five consonants in the third section.
These forms, both as individual parts and as a collective whole, constitute the Vidyā, which transcends all principles (tattvas) and possesses the nature of a limit (avadhi).

But surely it is well known and heard everywhere that the *kādividyā* alone possesses both natures, as in [passages] such as "Kāma, Yoni, Kamala," where "Ādi" refers to Brahmā, and "The second is Vāṇī," where "Ādi" refers to Speech. So how can it be said that the *hādividyā* alone possesses both natures? True. However, while the *kādividyā* is taught first in the *Upaniṣad* beginning with "Kāma, Yoni," the *hādividyā* is likewise extracted from that very same source. How so?

By such passages as, "The sixth, the seventh, and then the one whose charioteer is fire—causing these to enter the root-triad," and so forth, it follows that even the *hādi-vidyā* is indeed well-known in the Śruti. Therefore, it must be understood that it has been stated here that this very *hādi-vidyā* possesses a dual nature.
[Objection: In that case, if the *kādi-vidyā* also lacks this dual nature, there would be no inclination to adopt it. Why? Because of the difference in the deities.

How, then, is it established that only the *hādi* [vidyā] possesses this dual nature? To this it is replied: We do not say that the *hādi* vidyā alone is such and the *kādi* is not; rather, we have stated only this much—that the *hādi* alone is intended here, and not the *kādi*. This is because it is explained as such elsewhere. Indeed, the *kādi* vidyā also possesses this dual nature. The difference between these two vidyās is merely this: in the first section (*khaṇḍa*) of the *hādi*...

There are six vowels and six consonants. In the first section beginning with *ka*, there are seven vowels and five consonants. Taken together, in both *vidyās*, the first section consists of twelve syllables; thus, both *vidyās* indeed possess a dual nature. However, the method of practicing these two *vidyās* must be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru. The deity, like the mantra, likewise possesses this dual nature.

He states the identity of the mantra and the deity: "Vidyā also has such a nature. Vidyā is that whose essential nature is consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*). She has such a nature: she is the self of the universe (*viśvātmikā*) and yet transcends it; she is subtle and impossible to delimit. She is well-known in all the Vedāntas. Regarding the term *Tripurasundarī*: she is called *Tripurā* because she fills (*pūraṇāt*) all things existing in the three cities (*tripura*), and she is called *Sundarī* because she is desirable as the object of worship for all yogis. Thus, she is designated by the word *Tripurā*.

The etymological derivation has already been explained in detail. The noble ones (āryāḥ) maintain the absolute non-difference between the Goddess—who is of the nature of pure light and whose form consists of the play of emanating the universe—and Tripurasundarī, who is the fifteen-syllable mantra consisting of the supreme speech and knowledge. They maintain their eternal oneness and establish it everywhere. "The noble ones" means the supreme yogis, headed by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
Likewise, in the *Cidambararahasya*:
"I am directly the five-syllabled [mantra], while you are the fifteen-syllabled one.
And in the *Catuśśati*:
Whatever power is proclaimed for whatever object, that is the Goddess who is the sovereign of all; and that too is the Great Lord himself.
This Vidyā, consisting of fifteen syllables and embodying the qualities of the elements,
is pervaded by groups of five, six, and four syllables respectively.

"Distinguished by the division of vowels and consonants, she is divided into thirty-seven [forms]. Through the non-differentiation of those thirty-seven, she takes the form of the thirty-six *tattvas*, and yet her true nature transcends the *tattvas*; this *vidyā* is thus always contemplated.
This *vidyā* is fully expounded in the *Rahasyopaniṣad*, as follows: "The gods indeed said to Prajāpati..."

When the gods asked, "Who is this? What is her form? Of what color is she? What does she do? What does she give? By what means is she accomplished? What should we do?", Prajāpati replied. Having established the supremacy of the fifteen-syllabled mantra (*pañcadaśākṣarī*) through such statements as "She is not like this, she transcends the world, she is inconceivable, she is ineffable," he taught the venerable fifteen-syllabled mantra itself to the gods. We shall thus recite it: *Ādir ādibrahmā*.

The second *vāṇī* [is the first], the third is *māra*, then *mahendra*; this is the second [example] we shall cite as consisting of the lineage of the objects denoted by the earth (*bhū-vācya-dharma-santāna*). First is *ādirudra*, then that which consists of nectar (*sudhāmaya*), then the Lord of Creatures (*prajānām īśaḥ*), then the *haṃsa*. [Then the earth (*bhūmi*)]. Then this Self (*ātmā*); this is the lineage of the meanings of the names of the earth (*bhuvo nāmārtha-santāna*) consisting of enjoyment and bliss (*bhoga-ānanda-maya*). This is the third [example] we shall cite. At the beginning is the Lord of Life (*jīvaneśa*), then...

"Vāta is the creator of all; from that arises Lakṣmī, the mother of the world; from that arises the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), named Svarṇamedas, the wish-fulfilling gem consisting of both existence and non-existence.

Having taught this, he instructs: "This is the first quarter," thus teaching the first section; "We shall cite the second section," thus teaching the second section; and "We shall cite the third," thus teaching the third section. Having taught all of it—

He speaks of the majesty of that mantra: "She became manifold. This very one is the Great Mantra; she is this very body of sound (*śabdatanu*). She consists of all phonemes (*varṇa*), she is the supreme three-footed one, the state of the triple Veda (*trayī*). She is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), the form of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), eternal, stainless, faultless, beyond phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the pervasive knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*).
He who knows her as such becomes a wise man of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). Now they say: "The knowers [call her] 'Rahovī', the secret (*rahasya*). She is Śiva.

"This is Śiva, this is Śiva. He alone creates, protects, and withdraws these beings; he transforms them—making the minute great, the thin thick, the short long, the pervasive all-pervading. He is the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa), the venerable one. "He who knows thus becomes that very [Śiva]"—this is the meaning of this Vedic revelation (*śruti*). It is not written here as it is to be understood from the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*). Furthermore, the extraction of the *Hādi-vidyā* is mentioned in the *Rasasārasaṅgraha*. Some of the statements therein are written below: [The text continues with Sanskrit verses.]
I shall now correctly explain the ninth Vidyā in brief:
that of the Great Goddess Lalitā, beginning with "Mādana" and so forth in sequence.
Mādana, whose form is breath, is called Śiva as expansion;
the letter Sa, however, should be known as the other, contraction, which has the nature of Śakti.
Contraction is the supreme Śakti; expansion is Paramaśiva. Contraction and expansion are the two syllables of "Haṃsa.
As the substratum of these two, Bindumālinī must be established. Prāṇa is declared to be the Bindu, and by association, [it is so called] in relation to Apāna as well.
Then, the Earth-lord (L), the Sky (H), and the Fire (R) below those two; and the Māyā (Ī) with the Bindu (M) above—this is proclaimed as the Vāgbhava [Bīja]. As stated in the Śrī Haṃsaparameśvara:
"Mā is declared to be Śakti, while Śiva is the one who accepts the act of eating."
For that letter *ha* is called *mādana*, and it is designated as *Śiva*.
Just as his power (śakti) exists in the upward direction, the letter *sa* is prescribed for him;
Śiva is said to be the letter *ha*, while the letter *sa* is the imperishable power (śakti).
The supreme lord is a synonym for the syllable *kārṇa* (the letter *ka*) with a *bindu* and *mālinī*;
for the syllable consisting of *śakra* (the letter *la*), *vyoman* (the letter *ha*), and *anala* (the letter *ra*), there are *māyā*, *bindu*, *īśvara*, and so forth.
And as they truly exist, that is the reality; Vāgbhava is with wind and without wind.
"The other two syllables, known as Kāmaśakti, consist of the Niṣkala [form]"; thus it should be understood. Furthermore, the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Krodha has stated:
"Those three supreme *kūṭas*, manifested through the four ears (*catuḥśruti*), are indeed the Mūla, Vāgbhava, Mahāśrī, and Kāmarāja, known as the Shining Power (*sphuracchakti*)."
O Śivā, whose lovely red hue is known through the elements, the seasons, the Vedas, and the letters—
he who knows this is indeed the creator of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all worlds.
On this point there is a scriptural passage:
"Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech humans speak."
Scriptural passages such as these should also be considered. 18–19.
Having thus stated the non-difference between the *vidyā* and the deity, he describes the manner in which the *cakra* arises, in order to express the identity between the *cakra* and the deity:

"She who is the supreme Great Goddess (*maheśī*) whose form is the internal resonance (*antaroha*), whose nature is contemplated as threefold, who is manifest as the *paśyantī* and other [levels of speech], and whose essence is the three *mātṛkās*, has attained the state of the *cakra*. (20)
Even by the wise, not even a trace of difference is perceived between the Wheel and the Great Goddess;
for while these two appear gross, their subtle form is something entirely transcendent. (21)

The meaning of the term *cidvallī* is as follows: "Vallī" refers to that which has the nature of a creeper (*vallī*). "Antara" means the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Uha" means deliberation (*vitarka*). That whose form is accompanied by such [deliberation] that is devoid of limitation in the form of "it is thus"—that is the meaning. The sense is this: she is beyond the reach of speech and mind, indefinable by all the Vedāntas, and the cause of all.

The Great Goddess (Maheśvarī) is called "Supreme" (Parā) because she is the ground for the manifestation of the entire collection of principles (tattva-saṅghāta), beginning from Śiva and ending with the Earth; she is the most excellent. As the Yajurvedic scripture states:

"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold. And: "Whence words turn back, along with the mind, not having attained it—the bliss of Brahman, which the wise Brahmin knows. And as it is said in the Āgamas:

"The light of one's own essential nature (*svarūpajyotis*) alone is the supreme internal speech (*parāvāk*), which does not depart; when that [nature] is perceived, all worldly authority (*adhikāra*) ceases.
And the Laghubhaṭṭāraka says: "You are that certain Power (*śakti*) of inconceivable form and majesty, who is celebrated as the Supreme (*parā*).

She, characterized by being such, is that very Supreme Power. "Meditated upon in three ways" (*tribhāvitā*) means she has been meditated upon through a threefold mode, such that the state of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) has arisen.

He says this very thing: "That [power] is the clear one, consisting of the three mothers beginning with Paśyantī. By "clear," she is meant as that which has arisen first and takes the intended object as its domain; thus she is called *paśyantī*. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), *madhyamā* and *vaikharī* are included. That very power, known as *vaikharī*, consists of the form of articulate speech, comprises a collection of fifteen syllables, and is said to be the essence of the entire web of Vedic and Tantric words. Thus it is stated in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:

Victorious is she who, as *parā*, perceives the source of all births; as *paśyantī*, she is the vine from which clusters of blossoms arise; as *madhyamā*, she is the fragrance; and as *vaikharī*, she is the rosary of syllables.
Even in our own doctrine of the latent impression of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandavāsanā*), it is said:
"These three Mothers, consisting of the desire to speak, determination, and speech, are the very nature of the Great Goddess beginning with Paśyantī; there is no doubt in this."

Such is the nature of the one consisting of the three Mothers; she herself has attained the state of the *cakra*. This means the unity of the *cakra* whose essence is the three sections (*trikhaṇḍā*), and so forth.

He explains that very point: for the *cakra*—which consists of nine enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvānandamaya Bindu, and which serves as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Sundarī—the Great Goddess, and of Sundarī who is presided over by her—even the slightest trace of difference, even a slight distinction, is not perceived nor experienced by the wise, those who possess specific knowledge.

Why? Because the Śrīcakra is the very nature of Śrīsundarī. Thus, the Upaniṣad states: "The greatness of the deities is most vast; the nine sources have established the nine cakras. There are indeed nine yogas and nine Yoginīs. Of the nine cakras, there is one Mistress who possesses the nine mudrās and the nine auspicious [energies] of the great ones. She was the first, and she was the ninefold. And so forth. In the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
That pentad of powers arises through emanation, and the fourfold fire through dissolution;
from the union of the five powers and the four fires, the emergence of the wheel occurs.

Having begun with, "O fair-faced one, I shall now describe this descent of the Cakra, just as that Supreme Śakti [descends]," and ending with, "The Cakra is the form of Kāmakalā; its ultimate reality is expansion," the complete non-duality is established.
Krodhabhaṭṭāraka also says:
"The Śrīcakra is the churned essence of the root of the Vedas, consisting of the wheel of transmigratory existence," and so forth.

Furthermore, he distinguished such a difference between these two with the words beginning "of these two in their subtle form": the subtle nature of these two, namely the Cakra and the Deity, in their subtle forms...

You alone are the one whose nature is unlimited. In that regard, the subtle existence of the Śrīcakra as the essence of the *bindu*, and the limited nature of the *bindu* within the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) of the *bindu*, has already been elaborated upon by such statements as "in the *baindava* [space]... Furthermore, it has been stated regarding the Deity and the Vidyā as well, in passages such as "the Vidyā also has such a nature...
This applies likewise to the gross forms of the Cakra and the Deity. Here, "grossness" refers to the manifestation of the Cakra from the triangle (*trikoṇa*) up to the square (*caturasra*).

The contemplation of even the deity [Tripura] as being of the nature of another Tripura-shakti, such as Tripurambika and so forth—this is the meaning: because there is no distinction or differentiation between the two vidyās and their respective cakras and deities. He states the reason for this: "She is indeed that subtle-formed one. She is the one previously described by those characteristics; "indeed that" means she is the primordial Shakti herself.
"Subtle-formed" means that the form, which is the essential nature (svarūpa), of these two is subtle. Thus it has been said:
In the *Catuḥśatikā*:

"The *mātṛkā* is the source of the origin of the three worlds through the distinction between the gross and the subtle. For this very reason, even a slight difference is not perceived by those who know; for in this way alone is the contemplation of *vidyā* everywhere.

And thus says the Śruti: "All this, indeed, is Brahman. "Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self. Furthermore, the author of the text will state later on: "When this supreme Maheśī transforms herself into the form of the Cakra, that is the deity-nature of the Cakra. (20–21)

Beyond this, in order to describe the Śrīcakra— which consists of nine triangles (*navayoni*) and is the manifestation of the unfolding of the powers (*śakti*) such as Parā and Paśyantī— the author first states that the *bindu*-circle,
known as Sarvānandamaya, is composed of the power Parā: "In the center of the cakra, there shall be this very principle of the *bindu*, which consists of Parā."
And when that [which was] swollen has clearly transformed into the form of a triangle. || 22 ||
This triad, beginning with Paśyantī, is the primary cause and consists of three seed-syllables (bījas).
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are the portions that constitute the unsurpassed Ambikā.

The "Cidvallī" is explained as being the very same as previously described: the central point (*bindu-tattva*) arising from the center of the wheel consisting of the nine *yoni*s, whose nature is the *bindu*.
This, realized within oneself, is precisely the supreme (*parā*) essence, meaning it is the nature of Parā-Śakti. Thus it has been said: "It has issued forth..."
"The station of Viśvalaharī consists of the three Mothers; it is the Wheel of the Bindu (baindava-cakra). In that very same [text] it is said:
"The subtle form of all phonemes is the supreme vow, the supreme liṅga;
it is said to be the form of the Bindu, the bulb of supreme bliss."

Likewise, the nature of the Bindu (the Point) is the single life-force (*prāṇa*) of the six paths. In the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*, it is said that when this very reality of the Bindu attains a state of expansion, then the Triangle-Cakra arises: "And when that is swollen. This means that at this time, by the power of the unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, that Bindu-nature also becomes swollen—that is, it undergoes expansion—and then [it arises] in the form of a triangle.

The meaning is that it transforms into a triangular shape by means of the form of *anuttarānanda* (unsurpassed bliss) and *icchā-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic power of will). Thus it is said in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*: "The consciousness of unsurpassed bliss, when joined with the power of will, they call the triangle, beautiful with the bliss of emission (*vīsaraga*)."

"Having its radiance contracted by the expansions of the object, the subject, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing, it assumes the form of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic), which consists of will, knowledge, and action.
The meaning is that the form of *śṛṅgāra* is the triangle (*trikoṇa*). This triangle is the wheel (*cakra*), the source of the triad beginning with *paśyantī*; it is *paśyantī*.

The meaning is that the *madhyamā* [speech] is the cause for the arising of the triad of powers, headed by *vaikharī*. Likewise, it is stated in the *Subhagodaya-vāsanā*: "I contemplate the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*), known as Sattva and so forth, as the Great Triangle, the unsurpassed [teaching] from the mouth of the Guru."
Also in the *Pratyabhijñā*:

"In the case of entities that are the forms of one's own limbs, Māyā is indeed made threefold by the [powers of] being, knowledge, and action, as well as will; these are the sattva, rajas, and tamas of the bound soul (paśu)."

The powers of will, knowledge, and action themselves have attained the state of the triad of powers beginning with Paśyantī. For it is said: "The power of will is Vāmā, abiding in the form of Paśyantī;
the power of knowledge is Jyeṣṭhā, proclaimed as the speech of Madhyamā."
In the state of the universe's manifestation, she is renowned for her form consisting of straight lines;
yet, in the state of its withdrawal, she assumes the form of the Bindu.
"By the very sequence of return, this Raudrī, whose form is the Kriyā-śakti, is intensely radiant with the body of Śṛṅgāra, and is Vaikharī, whose physical form is the universe.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Tantrasadbhāva*.
That Mātṛkā who exists in the world, endowed with supreme splendor—
by her all this is pervaded, as far as the realm of Brahmā.

Beginning with these words and ending with “thus, that one [power] is born threefold,” the description of the web of powers such as Paśyantī and the others belonging to the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) has been provided. That [explanation] should be understood from that very source. However, it is not written here for fear of excessive length. As for the phrase “and having the form of the three seeds”:
the three seeds are the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti seeds, which consist of three parts (*trikhaṇḍa*). That [mantra] whose nature consists of those seeds is what is meant. And so:

The Śruti says: "Three cities, three paths, all-seeing, wherein the imperishable syllables are established; presiding over these ageless cities, the Great One is the majesty of the gods. By such passages, [the text] speaks of the divine Śṛṅgārapīṭha, which is the cause of the substratum of the Mātṛkā consisting of three parts (trikhaṇḍātmaka), the source of the manifestation of all mantras. Also, in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
"Furthermore, for the entire mantra endowed with the three seed-syllables,
these forms of the expressed [meaning] consist of Kula and Kaula.
Thus, the Lord Paramaśiva speaks of the triangle— which consists of the three seed-syllables, the three powers, and the three liṅgas— as being the form of the syllable Kāmakalā.

Then he says that this very reality of the *bindu* (the point), consisting of the venerable Supreme Goddess (*Śrīparābhaṭṭārikā*), became the *Śrīcakra*, which is composed of nine female generative organs (*yoni*) facing upward and downward:

"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and by the word 'and' (*ca*), Parāśakti as well—these five powers are portions of the Absolute (*anuttara*); these portions of the Absolute are the five downward-facing triangles within the *Śrīcakra*. The meaning is that they have come into being as such in reality."
Will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and the quiescent (*śāntā*)—these are the subsequent components;
whether taken individually or collectively, these two syllables constitute this *paśyantī* which consists of eleven aspects. (24)

The *cidvallī* consists of four powers—will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and the quiescent (*śāntā*)—which constitute its upper parts and take the form of four upward-facing triangles. The underlying sense is that these, which are the manifestations of the Supreme (*parā*), are Paśyantī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā; likewise, they are the upper parts.

These are Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), Action (kriyā), and Quiescence (śāntā). This wheel of nine triangles consists of this group of nine powers. This has been thoroughly described in the *Catuḥśatikā*, beginning with "When she perceives the vibration of the Self, that is the supreme digit," and ending with "Vaikharī, whose form is the universe. It should be understood from that very source as consisting of two groups of letters, both separate and non-separate.

"Vyasta" means the individual form; "avyasta" means the collective form. The meaning is that these two syllables, established here in all the Upanishads according to the principle of the "message," consist of all letters, are composed of the *mātṛkā* mantra, take the form of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and are the *bindu-tattva* consisting of the syllable *kāmākala*, which is pregnant with the state of perfect *ahantā* (I-consciousness).

Herein it is established by all the Agamas that this very *bindu*, consisting of perfect *ahantā* and distinguished as the consort of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*), alone is the accomplisher of all effects.

Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; he was of the form of a person (puruṣavidha). Having reflected, he saw nothing other than himself. He first uttered, 'I am. Thereupon, the name 'I' arose. Therefore even now, when addressed, one first says, 'It is I,' and then utters another name," it is taught that the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is fullness of *ahaṃtā* (I-ness), having assumed the form of the divine couple, shines forth as the creator of all principles (*tattva*).
It is concluded by the subsequent passage: "Verily, he had no delight; therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second.
He was so much as a man and woman in close embrace. He caused this very Self to fall into two parts.
From that, there came to be the husband and the wife," and so forth. Likewise, elsewhere in that same [text]: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."

"In the passage beginning with 'He, being alone, desired: "May I have a wife, and may I procreate; may I have wealth, and may I perform ritual action"—this much indeed is desire,' Brahman is understood as being accompanied by a consort. The meaning is that when those two classes [of phonemes] thus constituted, consisting of eleven, are combined and analyzed, they become elevenfold. This refers to the tenfold group of powers (śakti-daśaka), from *parā* to *śāntā*, in its individualized (*vyaṣṭi*) form.

And because it is the form of the totality of all things, it is one; thus, this very *bindu*-tattva, consisting of eleven aspects, is the power of Paśyantī as the cause. Just as in the statement, "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; therefore, one should meditate on it as peaceful," there is a designation of non-difference between the effect and the cause. || 24 ||

Henceforth, in order to describe the method of creating the wheels (*cakra*) such as the eight-petaled and ten-spoked ones, he concludes the sequence of the primary subject, the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*): "Thus, [the Goddess] consists of the *kāmakalā*, whose nature is the three points (*tribindu*), and who is composed of the phonemes that are the essence of reality."
This Mother, who has assumed the form of a triangle, is the very nature of the three qualities (guṇas). || 25 ||
"Cidvallī":

In the manner previously described, Kāma is the essence of the *kāmakalā*, whose sole nature is light (*prakāśa*), and who is the Supreme Śiva consisting of the syllable *Anuttara*. *Kalā*, however, consists of the final letter of all phonemes, which is the syllable of the *paramahaṃsa*; her form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). This state of being composed of both is innate.

It is the state of possessing a fully developed sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*). This has been clearly stated in the passage: "The *bindu* is of the nature of the *ahaṅkāra*. Of such a form, she is the essence of the *Kāmakalā*, whose own nature consists of the three *bindus*. The three *bindus* are, as previously mentioned, of the nature of the red, the white, and the mixed. Their essential character is the *tattva*. She is composed of those phonemes (*varṇa*)—such as the *Vāgbhava* and others—which have that very nature as their essence. Thus it is said in the *Rahasyāmnāya*:
"Know that one's own beautiful *śṛṅgāṭa* consists of three drops (*bindu*), which are white, red, and mixed, and are ancient, having the nature of the *praṇava*.
It is to be understood as consisting of three lines, dense with consciousness, and having the nature of Śiva. Of these, the red is without support; what remains from that is the beloved.
But in their union, the mixed is the stainless state of *nirvāṇa*. Thus [it is said].
In the *Catuḥśatikā*:

"Meditating upon the primordial Śakti, who consists of the three peaks (kūṭas), whose nature is both the totality and its individual parts, one considers this to be the true meaning of existence. Thus it is said.

This very [Consciousness], having assumed the form of a triangle, is the ultimate reality consisting of the mass of Consciousness and Bliss (*cidānandaghana*), the essence of all scriptural traditions (*āmnāya*). This "I-am-the-universe" (*viśvāham-bhāvanā*) is experienced as one's own witness by the most excellent great yogis. She is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)—desire (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*)—which consist of the power of *māyā*, namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and she is the embodiment of the fundamental principles (*tattva*). Indeed, it is by resting upon her that she performs the creation and other functions of the universe. And these qualities (*guṇa*) are themselves composed of the powers of desire, knowledge, action, and *māyā*.

Likewise, in the *Pratyabhijñā*, it is said: "In the forms of the dog's limbs, there is the reality (*tattva*)," and so forth. The qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are composed of will, knowledge, and action.

Therefore, the Mother, the creator of the entire universe, is the one Self; or, according to the manner stated in the Śruti, "In the beginning, this was indeed One alone," she is the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*) transcending all categories of existence (*tattvas*). She bestows all accomplishments (*siddhis*), according to the statement of the learned masters: "The triangle is the union of the Absolute (*anuttara*), Bliss (*ānanda*), and Will (*icchā*)."
The meaning is that she, who is identical with the universe, has entered the triangle-cakra which is the secret essence of Kādi;
as it is said in a scriptural passage:
"The Absolute Bliss (anuttarānanda) is joined to the power of will (icchā-śakti) within consciousness (citti)."
They call that triangle beautiful with the fragrance of the emission (vīsasga). || 25 ||
One is the supreme [power], while the other is the inferior, consisting of the individual manifestations such as Vāmā and the rest, whose nature is the creation of the Mothers.
By that [union], the Navātman was born; she is the Mother known by the names Madhyamā and the others.
Immediately thereafter, he states that the *madhyamā* [vāc] also possesses a ninefold nature through another classification:
"For the *madhyamā* is twofold: the subtle (*sūkṣmā*) and that which exists in a gross form (*sthūlākṛtisthitā*).
The subtle consists of the nine *nādas*, while the gross consists of the nine classes of phonemes and is known as the *bhūtalipi*. (27)

Regarding the phrase *cidvallī ekāparā*: he states that even Paśyantī and the others, which consist of the manifestation beyond this [Parā], possess a ninefold nature as the essence of the wheel of the nine *yonis*.

Another [form] is Vāmā, whose nature is the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) creation of the subjects; thus, she has become ninefold. Beyond that is Parā, who is the expansion [itself], while Paśyantī is the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) of Vāmā and the others.

Because she consists of the nine powers beginning with Vāmā and ending with Śāntā, which constitute the creation of the Mother (Mātṛsṛṣṭi), for that reason she is the Mother named Paśyantī, the progenitress.

The meaning is that the Navātmā, whose nature is the wheel of the nine wombs (*navayonicakra*), has become manifest—having arisen as the cause for the manifestation of the cluster of powers beginning with Vāmā and ending with Śāntā.

In this context, the definitions of these powers beginning with Vāmā are stated briefly by way of digression. Among them, the one called Vāmā is the [power] that [projects] the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) situated within herself.

Through the act of vomiting [impurities], she is called Viśvajanayitrī (the Mother of the Universe); Jyeṣṭhā is the bringer of all auspiciousness; Raudrī is the dispeller of all diseases; and Ambikā is the power that bestows all desired objects. And so says the Āgama:
"Vāmā is so called because she emits the universe; Jyeṣṭhā is so called because she consists of Śiva; Raudrī is the one who dissolves suffering and milks all karmas.
Thus, she is Ambikā, the radiance, the Great Being (mahāsattā). According to the state of Pratyabhijñā, she is the self whose nature is perfectly full and transcends all.
She is skilled in the vision of vibration (*sphuraṇa*). Thus, in the *Catuḥśatikā*: "When one perceives the vibration of the Self, that is the supreme *kalā*;

having attained the form of Ambikā, she is proclaimed as Parā Vāk. Furthermore, the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) are explained as being of the nature of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, as stated in the *Catuḥśatikā* with the words:
"The power of will should likewise be known as abiding in the form of Paśyantī," and so forth.

By such scriptural passages as "She is peaceful, partless, actionless, and tranquil," the power consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī śakti*) is shown to be unrestrained (*niraṅkuśā*). Thus the venerable Mṛtānandanātha explains it in the passage "Nāda and Bindu are partless" (*niraṃśau nādabindū*): "The power is unrestrained and peaceful; the partlessness of the peaceful [power] is due to its being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatvāt*). By the two designations beginning with "Madhyamā," the state of equilibrium between Madhyamā and Parā-Paśyantī is indicated.
By means of the two names. || 26 ||

She, known as the Middle (Madhyamā), is visible to the supreme yogins who are turned inward; she is a power (*śakti*) of two kinds, of two types, due to her gross and subtle states. Among these, the subtle is experienced through the state of *samādhi*. The gross exists as a continuous series of phonemes (*varṇāvalī*), which, by virtue of its gross form, is fit for the verbal expression of both the learned and the common folk. He explains this very point: "The subtle consists of the nine *nādas*; the gross consists of the nine groups (*vargas*)."

The meaning is this: from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, the Great Mātṛkā Kuṇḍalinī—consisting of manifold *nādas*—having pierced the lotuses beginning with the Svādhiṣṭhāna by means of the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*), approaches the lap of Paramaśiva seated upon the lotus of the *dvādaśānta*. She is experienced as one's own self by the great Mahāmaheśvaras who have attained all objects through *samādhi*. Thus says the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*: "She consists of nine *nādas*."

For example: "Now we shall explain the determination of the Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa. Having pointed out the Supreme Brahman as the Paramahaṃsa by means of the mantra 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa' and so forth to a celibate student who is self-controlled and devoted to the Guru, [the text] further specifies that meditation upon it: 'Having pressed the anus, having raised the vital air from the *ādhāra*, having circumambulated the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, having gone to the *maṇipūraka*, having passed beyond the *anāhata*, and having restrained the breaths in the *viśuddha* [cakra]... "

Having described a specific meditation upon the *brahmarandhra* with the words "running after the command, meditating [upon the *brahmarandhra*]," etc., he further explains that the nature of the *mūlakuṇḍalinī*, which pervades from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, consists of *nāda*: "When the *haṃsa* has dissolved, when the *nāda*— resembling pure crystal— from the *ādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, that indeed is Brahman."

The passages beginning with "He is called the Supreme Self" set forth the various constituent elements of its worship. He analyzes the *nāda* (sound): that arises in ten forms. The first is *ciṇī*; the second is *ciṇi ciṇī*; the third is the sound of a bell; the fourth is the sound of a conch; the fifth is the sound of a lute string; the sixth is the sound of cymbals; the seventh is the sound of a flute; the eighth is the sound of a kettle-drum (*bherī*); the ninth is the sound of a clay drum (*mṛdaṅga*).

The tenth is Meghanāda. Having abandoned the ninth, one should practice the tenth alone. When that has dissolved, when the mind has departed, and when conceptualization and discursive thought have been burnt, [one realizes] "I am Sadāśiva"—thus says the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*. From the phrase "When the Mūlādhāra is burnt, 'I am Sadāśiva'" in the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*, up to "In the Mūlādhāra, Maheśvarī... and ending with "...is not within the scope of Vedic injunction," there is the nine-fold group consisting of the letters *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, la*.
The gross [level] is said to be the object of all worldly transactions.
As it is stated in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"That which is Mātṛkā in the world, endowed with the supreme light—by her all this is pervaded, up to the end of the world of Brahmā."
O beloved, just as the sound (nāda) residing there pervades the world of the gods, and just as that which is without letters (avarṇastha) abides within all letters and is omnipresent,
so shall I explain clearly to you for the sake of certain understanding.
Beginning thus:
"That power which is supreme, subtle, and said to be formless,
having coiled around the bindu of the heart, remains in a state of deep sleep in the form of a serpent."
There, the great yogi, sleeping, perceives nothing—
the moon, the sun, the wind, the stars, nor the fourteen worlds.
When her belly was pervaded by that, the goddess fell into a stupor like one who has consumed poison;
she, whose nature is knowledge, was awakened by a supreme sound.
Churned by the fire residing within the belly even from its bond,
the churning of the Śakti’s form proceeds through the movement of that very rotation.
But from the first arising of differentiation, the bindu attains the state of nāda;
by that [process], Kuṇḍalī, who is subtle as Time, arises.
The Bindu, consisting of four parts, is the Lord who resides above Śakti;
O Dear One, through the yoga of churning the center, straightness is produced.
That power is remembered as Jyeṣṭhā, well-centered between two points (bindus).
Through the line, Amṛtakuṇḍalī attains the state of Bindu and Nāda.
She is to be known by the name Lākinī; she possesses both bindus as they have come together. She is declared to be three-footed and is celebrated by the name Raudrī.
She is seen as the Obstructress because she obstructs the path to liberation;
Ambikā has the form of a crescent of the moon and is the light of the half-moon.
Thus, this single supreme power (parā-śakti) is born as threefold;
from these [powers], both when conjoined and when distinct, the group of nine is produced.
"And it is remembered as ninefold, characterized by the nine groups.
Here, someone, having fabricated the reading "subtle, gross, form, and stable," says: "It is subtle, stable, gross, and consists of the nine groups.

This being the case, the word "nine groups" lacks syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), and there is a violation of the traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*). That person, however, not knowing the tradition, [speaks] according to his own intellect.
He spoke for this purpose: therefore, the propriety of the meaning stated by us and the meaning stated by him is to be understood only by learned scholars who possess specialized knowledge;
enough said on this point. Regarding the term *bhūtalipi* (elemental scripts): these are both elements (*bhūta*) and scripts (*lipi*).

Here, the "elementality" (*bhūtatva*) of the scripts consists in their being accessible through specific arrangements. And that [accessibility] is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because syllables consist of the power whose nature is light (*tejas*).

And thus says the scripture: "That Mātṛkā which exists in the world is endowed with supreme splendor," and so forth: "All mantras consist of phonemes (varṇa), and they, O Dear One, consist of Śakti. || 27 ||

Regarding this, some explain that the name of these two is "the delusive script" (*bhrāntilipi*). However, because that would result in a metrical defect (*chandobhaṅga*), it is unacceptable and should be disregarded.
For the subtle-form *madhyamā* is indeed one, having attained the state of being the cause of the gross-form [speech]. Therefore, he says:
"Since the former is the cause and the other is the effect between these two, for that reason..."
This very [nature] is this [effect]; indeed, there is no difference, for identity is held to exist between cause and effect. (28)
The *cidvallī* is the first, being the aforementioned subtle cause because it is the first to arise. The other is the gross effect, being the result produced from that [cause].
Therefore, from that cause—namely, from the existence of these two, the subtle and the gross, as cause and effect—for that reason, by that cause.

This gross [form] is indeed that same subtle power; for there is no difference—indeed, difference does not exist at all. To the objection, "How can there be the relation of cause and effect in the absence of difference? he says: "Identity is desired between the cause and the effect. Identity consists of both difference and non-difference. The cause and the effect—that which possesses the nature of the produced and the producer—is accepted as being like clay and a jar, because they are merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātratvāt*). A single reality itself becomes twofold. Thus, according to all Vedānta...
The meaning is "it is agreed upon. || 28 ||

Immediately following, through the description of the wheels (cakras) beginning with the eight-cornered one, which consist of the expansion of the splendor of the erotic energy (*śṛṅgāratejas*) in the center, he describes the manifestation of the power of articulated speech (*vaikharī-śakti*):
"That eight-cornered [wheel] consists of the *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *pa* groups; it is the expansion of the central corner.
The center is the nine-cornered [wheel]. In this tenfold [group], illuminated by the lamp of consciousness (*ciddīpa*), [the power manifests]. (29)

The *cidvallī* [describes] that wheel called "Remover of All Diseases" (*sarvarogahara*), which consists of the *śa-ṣa-sa-pa* group of consonants; it has eight corners composed of the *śa-ṣa-sa-pa* group, its expansion being the width of the central triangle,
and thus it is a nine-cornered figure including the central corner, the center of which is known as the *bindu*.

The meaning is that she is illuminated by the mass of radiance of Tripurā— the embodiment of light— who, according to the stated method, is mounted upon the Bindu-cakra (the wheel of the point) as "the consciousness-element [situated] in the wind of the Saṃvarta [fire], established on the seat of the Bindu," within this aggregate of ten consisting of the Bindu, the Triangle, and the Eight-spoked [wheel], which is kindled by the lamp of consciousness.
Its shadow is this twofold [array], expanded in the form of two ten-spoked wheels,
with the extension of its clearly defined corners shining through the four groups of peripheral circles.
"cidvallī":
"this pair of its shadows"—meaning the pair of shadows, that is, the pair of radiances, of that aforementioned triad of wheels consisting of a mass of light;
[appearing] as two ten-spoked wheels, in the form of an inner ten-spoked and an outer ten-spoked wheel, as an infinite circle of light.
His two-fold luster has transformed into the nature of a pair of wheels known as the "Protector of All" (Sarvarakṣā) and the "Accomplisher of All Aims" (Sarvārthasādhaka); this is the meaning.
Thus it has been said:
"The ten-spoked [wheel] whose form is the radiance shimmering from the nine triangles. || 30 ||

He explains the nature of those two wheels: the inner ten-spoked wheel consists of the ten syllables comprising the *ta* and *ca* groups, while the outer ten-spoked wheel consists of the ten syllables comprising the *ca* and *va* groups; this is the meaning.
This transformation of the ten spokes is accompanied by the radiance of these four wheels.
This [maṇḍala] consists of fourteen spokes and is composed of the fourteenth letter belonging to the group of initial vowels. || 31 ||

"Cidvallī" refers to the fourfold wheel consisting of the Bindu, Triangle, Eight-spoked Wheel, and Inner Ten-spoked Wheel; its "prabhā" is its radiance or splendor. It is "endowed with" or joined to that.

"The transformation of the ten-spoked wheel" means the outer ten-spoked wheel (bahirdaśāra-cakra); the intended meaning is that this occurs because of the proximity of the four wheels beginning with the Bindu to the outer ten-spoked wheel.

In this context, the meaning is that its radiance pervades [them]. Thus it has been said: "Through transformation, it is joined with the form of the radiance of the four wheels. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Endowed with the radiance of this group of four wheels—consisting of the triangle, the eight-spoked wheel, and the two ten-spoked wheels—it is the eight-spoked wheel which is the transformation of the ten-spoked wheel, being possessed of the splendor of the ten-spoked wheel. He says the same thing: "The collection of the first vowels..."

"Consisting of fourteen phonemes and having fourteen spokes"—this means the wheel (cakra) known as the "Bestower of All Prosperity," which consists of the fourteen phonemes beginning with *a* and is endowed with fourteen corners. Thus, by means of the description of the wheels starting from the Bindu and ending with the sixteen-cornered [wheel], he states that the Vaikharī power has become manifest. || 31 ||

And by means of the supreme (parā), the visionary (paśyantī), and the intermediate (madhyamā) which consists of the forms of gross phonemes— through these, the *vaikharī* speech, composed of fifteen syllables, was produced.

The *cidvallī* and the characteristics of the powers beginning with Parā have already been explained extensively. This is the meaning: [Vaikharī] consists of the entire collection of phonemes from *A* to *Kṣa*, is the creator of the whole phenomenal world, and is composed of all sounds; she is Vaikharī. And so it has been said: "Vaikharī is the universal form," as expressed by the word *vāc* (speech) in the mouth.
"I take refuge in your Vaikharī speech, which is clear through the organs of articulation," and so forth. || 32 ||
From this point forward, he states that the two wheels named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa and Sarvāśāparipūraka consist of the phonemes of the *vaikharī* speech:

"One should contemplate this pair of eight-petaled lotuses, the former augmented by the eight letters beginning with 'ka' and the latter by the groups of *vaikharī* consonants, both combined with the collection of vowels. (33)

The *cidvallī* is correctly described as being fully augmented by the eight groups of *vaikharī*, which are the very nature of the *vaikharī* power, beginning with the letter *ka*. It is the eight-petaled lotus, the wheel that agitates all (*sarvasaṅkṣobhaṇacakra*). Likewise, it is endowed with the collection of vowels; that is, it is joined with the sixteen phonemes beginning with the vowel *a*.

The meaning is that this lotus with two sets of eight petals, which is being clearly visualized, should always be meditated upon as the wheel that fulfills all aspirations, having contemplated it correctly. || 33 ||
The three circles, consisting of the threefold light composed of the three drops, abide as the transformation of the triad;
this triad of earth-mandalas is the repose in the three Mothers, Paśyantī and the others.

The *cidvallī* verses are situated upon the eight-petalled lotus above the *manvaśra*, and upon the sixteen-petalled lotus above that. The three *bindus* consist of the previously mentioned red, white, and mixed [energies]. That triad of splendors consists of the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; "its modification" means they are composed of those [energies].
In this context, by stating that the three circles consist of the three fires, it is declared that the wheel is composed of three segments (*trikhaṇḍa*) whose nature is the moon, the sun, and fire.
As the scripture says:
"The *mātṛkā*-wheel has three segments and consists of the moon, the sun, and fire."
In the *Subhagodaya*:
"I meditate immediately upon the three eyes, which consist of the triad of energies— Soma, Sūrya, and Kṛśānu— the self-luminous fire— as the three circles."

And their modification—that is, those [geometrical] figures—should be understood as being like the statement "the Vedas are the authority" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*). The three circles of the earth are the abode of the multitude of powers (śaktis), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, the *brāhmī* and the rest, and the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* and the rest; they are the resting place of the three Mothers, Paśyantī and the others. The meaning is that these powers—Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī—expanding up to this point, shine forth in the form of the Śrīcakra, from the triangle up to the [circles of the] earth. And this...

Beginning with the words, "When one perceives the vibration of the Self, that is the supreme *kalā*," and ending with the passage, "Vaikharī has the universe as her form," this entire collection of texts has thoroughly established [the nature of speech]. || 34 ||
Stepping is the casting of the foot; by that, the arising [of the lineage] is described as twofold.
This covering consists of the two rows of Gurus, O Mother, which is the expansion of the lotus-feet.

From the words “cidvallī” up to “even the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*,” etc.: "kramaṇa" means the stepping of the feet (*padakrama*). That is twofold: consisting of the physical movement of the foot (*padavikṣepa*) and consisting of the arising of the sequence (*kramodaya*). Among these, what is called "the movement of the foot" is the capacity of Sundarī to generate infinite powers consisting of infinite millions of rays.
And likewise, the Upaniṣad says:
"The rays of Svayambhū which fashioned the bodies," and so forth;
and "While He alone shines," and so forth. And according to the Āgama:
She is the form of light, supreme in nature; and from her body indeed arise rays numbering a thousand, two thousand, and a hundred thousand.
Ten million times ten million is the highest number known for these;
by entering into that very [number], all that is moving and unmoving shines forth.
By the light of that Goddess Maheśānī, everything shines;
yet nothing exists devoid of Her being, nor does even desire manifest apart from it.
And without that [Supreme], the primordial nature of Śiva’s power, which is of the form of consciousness,
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings would certainly not come into existence;
O Maheśvarī, [this is true] of those infinite millions of rays.
"O Goddess Śivā, in the center there are three hundred and sixty rays;
O Pārvatī, these illuminate both the macrocosm (brahmāṇḍa) and the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa)," and so forth.
"The rays of consciousness, dwelling in all seats (pīṭhas), are omnipresent," and so forth.
One should worship the wheel of rays all around, bowing with devotion. Thus says Amṛtānanda:

"The *Kramodaya* is the emanation of the Śrī Guru—who consists of the infinite light and takes the form of the divine, perfected, and human lineages—as the mandala of the Gurus. Likewise, in the *Rahasyāmnāya*: 'The rays of the moon and sun from the two feet are indeed the Gurus. This will be explained further below.

It is elaborated as follows: he explains this very same twofold sequence—the *āvaraṇa* (enclosure) is the multitude of powers (*śakti-nikurumba*) situated within the wheel of enclosures, according to the logic of the expression "the platforms are shouting.

The *gurupaṅkti* (lineage of gurus) is the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*). These two constitute the expansion of the lotus-feet of the Mother; that is, the expansion, the spreading forth, the blossoming of the lotus-feet—the venerable pair of feet—of Ambā, who is Tripurā.

The *Yajuḥśruti* states: "Luminous, radiant, and majestic," and so forth. Likewise, the statement of an authoritative source says: "The great splendor of Tripura is described through many millions of divisions; in its center is the supreme, blazing Mahātripurasundarī."
And in the Ṣaḍanvaya-Śāmbhava:
"All [the goddesses] have hands granting boons and fearlessness, with bodies whose left halves are female;
they are of the nature of radiant energy (tejas) and should be meditated upon as supreme by those who solely desire liberation. (35)
He gradually explains the expansion of that [power]:
"When this Supreme Maheśī transforms into the form of a wheel, then the transformation of the limbs of her body becomes all the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās). (36)
That Goddess Tripurasundarī was seated upon the wheel consisting of the *bindu*,
her abode being the body of Kāmeśvara, and her crest-ornament fashioned from a digit of the moon.
Her own hands are adorned with a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, and arrows of flowers;
her body is as red as the rising sun, and she possesses three eyes—the moon, the sun, and fire.

This very "Cidvallī" (the Creeper of Consciousness) consists of an unbounded mass of light; she is the Supreme Goddess, the most excellent of all, who is adored by hosts of infinite millions of Yoginīs, and who takes pride in the sovereign wealth of her own self, which consists of eternal, limitless, and unsurpassed bliss. As stated in the Yajurveda: "From whence indeed... and so forth. And thus it has been said:
"Sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great power, honored by heroes, abide having taken refuge in this wheel. Thus it is said in the *Lalitopākhyāna*. And:
