Beyond the range of speech and indeed beyond the range of the intellect, it cannot be conceptualized as having such-and-such a form, being peerless and without equal;
they touch that supreme pride of sovereignty over the wheel, which contains the three worlds within it and is filled with all-pervading power.

"Thus in the form of a wheel"—this wheel consists of nine aspects, being the Mātṛkā divided ninefold. "Thus, as the ninefold wheel consisting of all-bliss, beginning with the Bindu and ending with Trailokyamohana," one should perceive the radiance of the Self; thus, at the time of beholding the Self which consists of full bliss, one should transform [one's state]. One should assume another form; the optative suffix (*liṅga*) is used in the sense of a prayer, because the manifestation of the mere outline of the universe is the object of that prayer.

The Brahman is designated by the very scripture concerning transformation (*pariṇāma-śruti*), as follows: having introduced the process of creation with the words, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" it continues, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing. Having entered into it, He became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*); the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*); the supported (*nilayana*) and the unsupported (*anilayana*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) and unconsciousness (*avijñāna*); truth (*satya*) and falsehood (*anṛta*). He became the Truth. And there is also *Smṛti*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "When this has matured" (*asyāṃ pariṇatāyām*): her body parts—her body being Tripurasundarī, whose nature is a mass of radiance, and its parts being rays—their maturation is the attainment of another state; here, these are the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatāḥ*), the multitude of powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vaśinī and ending with Aṇimā.
This [multitude] is essentially an ocean of consciousness and bliss, just as foam, bubbles, and waves arise from the ocean.
The meaning is that those possessing infinite powers undergo manifestation and disappearance. Thus, the Upaniṣad says:
"In whom all beings dissolve, and having dissolved, they again attain manifestation;
and once more they become unmanifest, being born again like bubbles."
And in the *Catuḥśatī*: "Such is the supreme splendor, abiding in the form of the Śrīcakra,
completely enveloped by the smoke-like radiance of its mass of powers."
Also, in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:
"Having contemplated the Yoginīs, beginning with Prakaṭā, within the sovereign wheel (*cakrarāja*),
they are situated respectively as waves in the ocean of consciousness known as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)."
"I worship these Yoginīs of the splendor of the mass of consciousness, who have shone forth from the Lord of the Cakra (Cakreśvara), and who have taken refuge in each respective Cakra. Thus,
beginning the description of the nature of the powers (śaktis) of the Vaśinyādi enclosure, he first describes the nature of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) with the words "āsīnā" and so forth.

Because it is stated that "in the *baindava* supreme space, which consists of the *bindu* and is called 'consisting of all bliss' (*sarvānandamaya*), [the Goddess resides]"; and because it is said in the *Rahasyopaniṣad*: "That upon which she moves is the *cakra*. Seated in the upper region, shining brilliantly, she is Tripurasundarī—unconditioned by place, time, or form, whose nature is that very [supreme space]. She is desirable as the cause of all.

The Goddess Svabhāvā, who dispels all activities such as the creation of the universe and so forth, whose abode is the lap of Kāmeśvara—that is, she whose dwelling place is the region of the beautiful left thigh of Śrīnātha, the Lord of Desire. Thus it has been said by Paramaśiva:
"Kalā, Vidyā, and Parāśakti, whose form is the shape of the Śrīcakra."
In the center of that is the station of Bindu; there dwells the Supreme Goddess.
"United with Sadāśiva, she is the virtuous one who transcends all principles (tattvas).
And elsewhere:
"The support of the radiance of the universal form, whose own nature is identical with Śiva."
"Seated upon the lap-couch of Kāmeśvara, exceedingly beautiful. Thus [it is said]. And Śrīnāthānanda says:
"Seated upon the left lap of the primordial Śrīgurunātha."

The Goddess, who delights in divine activities such as the creation of the universe, is said to have been fashioned from a digit (*kalā*) of the Moon. Here, by the word "fashioned" (*kalpita*), the Blessed Lady’s status as the instrument of the Moon’s play (*līlopakaraṇatva*) is indicated.

Her own hands are adorned with a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and five flower-arrows. Thus, the noose is the Will (*icchā*), which serves as the means for binding and uniting the distinctions of one's own nature.

The nature of Śakti is as follows: the *aṅkuśa* (goad) consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which is the means for shattering the distinctions of one's own nature. The five sugarcanes and bows consist of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is the instrument for abandoning forms distinct from one's own self. This is the meaning: by His command, the powers of will, knowledge, and action themselves assume the form of the fetters (*pāśa*) and so forth, and thus perform their worship. Accordingly, it is said in the *Catuḥśatī*:

"Holding the noose consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti) and the goad consisting of the form of knowledge (jñāna-rūpin), while bearing the arrow and bow consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), she is resplendent. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:

"I worship the supreme powers known as the weapons, beginning with Bāṇa, which are the causes for manifesting the differentiation of the Goddess’s existence as pure consciousness. Thus [it is said]. Her body is reddened like the rising sun; she resembles the rising sun; she possesses the triad of eyes consisting of the moon, the sun, and fire; she is composed of the moon, the sun, and fire, having three eyes.
And so it has been said:

"O Dear One, [one should meditate upon] the auspicious Goddess who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, who possesses four arms and three eyes, and who holds a noose, a goad, and a bow. (36–38)

This very divine couple, in the form of the assembly of gurus (gurumaṇḍala) undifferentiated by distinctions despite being divided by differences, is to be worshipped as that couple existing within the three-eyed [Lord] who consists of the three *bindus*, through the differentiation of qualities;
it is expanded out as the nature of the three pairs, beginning with Kāmeśī and Mitrāṃśa. 39.
"Cidvallī":
That couple is the couple consisting of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī, which is renowned in all the Upaniṣads as being beyond all things.
This is the meaning: the Supreme Self, having made His very own self consist of female and male, assumes the form of a couple and sports.

Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (Śruti): "He was alone and did not find delight; therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second [self]. He became as large as a man and woman in close embrace. He caused this Self to fall apart into two parts. From that, there arose the husband and the wife. Beginning thus, it continues until: "Whatever pair exists here, even down to the ants, he creates all that."
He states that Brahman is by nature disposed to sport in the form of a couple (*mithuna*). Likewise, the *Rahasyāgama* says:
"Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, [Brahman] is himself Sadāśiva.
Thus, he explains that the entire Tantra emerged from Paramaśiva alone, who has become a couple through the nature of Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*).
Thus, that couple consists of Mitrēśanātha and Kāmeśvarī, Śrīmad-Uḍḍīśanātha and Vajreśvarī, and Ṣaṣṭhīśanātha and Bhagamālinī.

The meaning is that the triad of couples is expanded— that is, extensively spread— through these three primary couples in the form of the lineages (krama) beginning with the Divine (divya), the Siddha, and the Human (mānava).

And this I shall fully elaborate in the passage: "In the Kṛta Yuga, the Guru Śiva, seated upon the Śrīpīṭha, [bestowed] the Vidyās. This meaning is also perfectly set forth in the *Rahasyopaniṣad*: "In the center is the Cakra; in the Bindu is the world of manifestation (*prapañca*); the world is the body in the form of Nada; the power (*śakti*) consists of the object; the Cakra is the body, the Bindu is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in the center is the Power—thus the quality (*guṇa*) along with its manifestation, the quality..."

The *liṅga* is threefold, distinguished as *svayambhū* (self-manifested) and so forth, and it bestows victory upon those who possess the three *liṅgas*. It takes forms according to desire, and Kaivalya, Uḍyāna, Pūrṇagiri, and Jālandhara are where the Goddess is of the nature of *sattva*.
Herein may this explanation be given—just as Nīlakaṇṭha spoke to Śamīgarbha: "From whence indeed these beings [arise]..."
"By which those born are produced and by which they live, and into which they enter when they depart—He asks: that which is seen here has Bliss as its source;

by that alone one lives, for that alone is life. With these words, beginning with "That is declared in this verse," the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire phenomenal world from Tripurā alone are established, preceded by a description of the Tripurā-cakra; and thus, she is the bestower of all fruits.

It is thus stated that Tripura alone is to be worshipped by heroes in the form of the Śrī Devīs. Likewise, the Rahasyāgama says: "Only by one whose final birth has occurred, or who is Śaṅkara himself, is this glorious fifteen-syllable Vidyā obtained. (39)

From here on, he describes the nature and manifestation of the deities of the enclosure: "Those who dwell in the eight-petaled [lotus], beginning with Sandhyā, Aruṇā, and Vaśinī, are this very *puryaṣṭaka* of the Goddess, whose body is the wheel and whose self is consciousness. (40)

The eight powers, beginning with Vaśinī, who reside in the eight corners of the *cidvallī* and whose nature is to dwell in the wheel known as the "Remover of All Diseases," are capable of bestowing the gift of the perfect sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*). How so? In this context, being the "remover of disease" means precisely the conferral of the perfect sense of "I-ness. [For] that which is incomplete—

Because it is said, "Let it be considered that disease is the ground for the sole cause of wretchedness," and because it is stated by the most learned, "These [mantras] specifically remove all diseases; reflect upon them thus," such are those Sandhyāruṇās, meaning they shine with a reddish form. For this very reason, this eight-cornered wheel (cakram) is near to the self of consciousness (*saṃvidātmanaḥ*); she whose own nature is knowledge itself, according to the Vedic statement: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."

The scripture and the tradition [state] that the Goddess was self-manifested from the very beginning. The meaning is that the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)—the subtle body—belongs to the Goddess, whose nature is to expand as "May I be many," who has the wheel as her form, and whose essence is the wheel. Thus it has been said:
"Consciousness (*citi*), the mind (*citta*), sentience (*caitanya*), and the twofold cognition (*cetana*)."
"The individual soul (jīva) and its body of powers (kalā), which is subtle, constitutes the *puryaṣṭaka*. And Śivānanda says:
"This entry into the eight spokes [of the wheel] occurs at the beginning of the departures of consciousness."
"The subtle city-of-eight [enters] the Goddess, without distinction and without weight. Thus [it is said]. (40)

Those functions directed toward that object, having attained the very nature of the Omniscient One and others, shine within the abode of the eight spokes, possessing forms as beautiful as the autumnal moon. (41)

The *cidvallīs* are the mental modifications (*vṛttis*) directed toward that [object]; they reside near the eight-petaled lotus (*vasukoṇa*). They are renowned for maintaining the state of identity with one's own Self.

Having attained the form of the ten powers (*śaktis*), such as omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and the rest, they dwell within the inner ten-spoked lotus (*antardaśāra*) and are mounted upon the wheel known as the "All-Protecting" (*sarvarakṣākara*).
The Yoginīs of the Inner Essence (nigarbha) possess forms as beautiful as the autumn moon, with appearances white and clear in their luminosity; they gleam and shine.
Thus it has been said:
"The auspicious goddesses residing within the inner decagon resemble a mass of lightning."
Those known as the Nigarbhas should be worshipped; they provide protection from all [evils]. || 41 ||
In the outer rows and corners of that [mandala] are the Yoginīs who bestow all siddhis;
they consist of the goddesses, the intellect, the organs of action, and their objects, and are richly adorned with bright garments and ornaments. (42)

"Cidvallī" refers to the outer rows and corners; that is, in the outer regions of that Sarvarakṣākara-cakra, specifically in the rows and corners situated above. This is because the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra consists of those very corners. The Yoginīs residing there are named Kulakaula.

The powers (śaktis) mentioned first are the bestowers of all accomplishments; they are the foremost givers of all siddhis. They consist of the objects of the goddess’s organs of cognition and action. The organs of cognition and action of the goddess Tripurā are the sense organs of knowledge, such as hearing, and the organs of action, such as speech. Their objects are sound and so forth, as well as speaking and so forth; "consisting of those" means having those as their essential nature. They are richly adorned with bright attire and ornaments; "bright" means having a radiant, white appearance.

They are richly endowed with both dress and ornaments. This is the meaning: the deities of the mantras, whose nature is non-dual, who bestow supernatural powers (*siddhi*), and who possess transparent forms, appear resplendent in white ornaments. Thus it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
"White, with hands displaying the boon and fearlessness gestures, and adorned with white ornaments."
Because they possess the nature of their own radiance through yoga, these mantras are designated by names that correspond to their actual meaning.
"Indeed, [the goddesses] beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā reside in the wheel that accomplishes all aims.
And in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:
"This external portion of ten spokes is the domain of the intellect, the organs of action, and the senses. (42)

The Yoginīs of the Oral Tradition (Saṃpradāya) are to be meditated upon as flashing forth from the cavities of the imitation of the goddess Bhuvanāra-cakra-bhavana-devī, clothed in garments the color of twilight. 43.

"Cidvallī" refers to those whose world-structure wheel (*bhuvanāracakra*)—the wheel that bestows all auspiciousness—is their abode or dwelling place. Within the Goddess, there are fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*): the five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, and the four known as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*).

In the *Pratyabhijñā*, however, it is stated that there are thirteen, consisting of the ten faculties of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the series of external and internal organs (*bāhyāntaḥ-karaṇāvali*). There, the number thirteen is mentioned excluding the mind (*citta*);

here, however, the number fourteen is mentioned including the mind. Regarding the phrase "in the Śrīpīṭha which consists of the mind": since the mind is also enumerated as an internal organ by the learned authorities, those [energies] whose manifestation—which serves as their commentary or exposition—takes the form of the fourteen spokes are so described.
The meaning is that the Goddess herself exists as the deity of the fourteen-spoked wheel (*cakra*), which consists of the fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*). Thus it has been said by Śivānanda:
"I remember the fourteen paths of the fourteen spokes, the fourteen-fold forest of Śiva belonging to the Great Goddess."

Those whose garments are of the same color as the twilight—that is, whose clothes resemble it—are the *sampradāyayoginīs*, the goddesses of the true tradition who consist of the primordial power (*ādiśakti*), beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the others; they are to be meditated upon, that is, they are to be properly contemplated as the "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Thus, it is said in the *Catuḥśatī*:
Because she has issued forth as the very essence of power (śakti), Maheśvarī resides in the wheel that bestows good fortune, having descended through the sequence of the tradition.
The auspicious goddesses, whose names correspond to their true meanings, resemble Aṇimā in their continuous nature as light, beauty, fortune, and power.
"Preceded by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, she bestows purity through the identity of the body and so forth. (43)

Having assumed the forms of women through the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), and the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), these most secret Yoginīs are victorious upon the lotus of the elephant’s skin (the forehead). 44.
*Cidvallī*.

The Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the principle (*tattva*) known as the Unmanifest. "The Great" (*mahat*) is the principle of the Great (*mahattattva*). "I-making" (*ahaṅkṛti*) is the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*). The subtle elements (*tanmātrā*) are the five subtle elements of the gross elements, beginning with earth. Taken together, these are eight. Those whose form or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is assumed by these [eight] mean that they are of the nature of the Goddesses. They are known by the names of the most secret Yoginīs because they constitute the innermost essence of the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*). Of these [Yoginīs], Anaṅgakusumā and the others—
Those whose designation is "most secret" are the eight powers beginning with Anaṅgakusumā.
They triumph—that is, they exist in a state of supreme excellence—within the eight-petaled lotus called Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, which is the second lotus [of the Vāgbhava-aṣṭaka]. Thus it was said by Śiva:
Possessed by the passion of the experience of the Kaulikas, they reside within the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city of the subtle body),
consisting in their essential nature of the subtle group of sounds associated with the eight *vāgbhava* syllables.
In the world, there are others who are even more secret, known as Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī;
they are Anaṅgakusumā and the rest, adorned with red bodices.
"Beautiful ones with hair arranged in braids, bearing bows and arrows. And Śivānanda says:
"This Lord, whose vehicle is the bull, who has the lotus as his emblem, and who holds the discus."
I determine that the unmanifest and other principles are the primordial natures (prakṛtis) of all beings.
The eight powers, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, triumph— that is, they exist in preeminence— within the eight-petaled lotus called Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, which is situated upon the elephant-hide covering.
From the sixteen-petaled lotus arises the enjoyment consisting of the senses and the mind.
I consider it to have attained the nature of a transformation of the Goddess. || 45 ||

The "cidvallī" consists of the elements, earth and the rest; the ten sense organs, from hearing to speech; and the mind, which is the primary internal organ. Having combined these sixteen, what is the nature of the Goddess’s office (*adhikāra*) as a distinct state of being? Why [is it so]?
And that Goddess, known as Vimarśa, has attained a fivefold state through the division of ether,
air, fire, water, and earth.

According to such statements, this wheel (cakra) named the "Fulfiller of All Wishes" consists of sixteen spokes and possesses sixteen such [deities]. It presides over—meaning it occupies—the forms of Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others by way of their sixteen powers (*śakti*). By the rule *adhi-śīṅ-sthā-āsāṃ karma*, these are treated as objects.
The meaning is that within this "Fulfiller of All Wishes" wheel, these Guptayoginīs, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī, reside as the essence of the vowels.
And so it is said in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
"The sixteen digits (*kalā*) consist of the wonder of the assembly of the sixteen vowels;
they are the sixteenfold nature of the sixteen principles (*tattva*), beginning with *prāṇa*."
Because they possess the nature of the seed-syllables which have become the essence, these [energies] take the form of seeds;
as the innermost limbs, the Guptayoginīs are well-established.
O Dear One, [the mantras] beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpākarṣaṇī are primarily characterized by emanation (sṛṣṭi).
In the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:
"I contemplate the lotus arising from sixteen petals, which consists of the senses and the mind as objects of enjoyment, and which has attained the nature of transformation. (45)
All these mudrās, together with the Trikhaṇḍā, are composed of pure consciousness and are fully elevated;
they resemble the primordial earth, the dwelling of the household, and the luster of the rising sun.
By which her ninefold support is transformed into the form of nine wheels, and by which the powers of the nine lords are likewise transformed into the form of mudrās. || 47 ||
Together with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā known as the *trikhaṇḍā*, they exist in supreme excellence; they dwell in the primordial abode of the earth, residing in the primary square.
By their radiance, they are equal to the splendor of the rising sun, possessing the luster of fresh dawn; they consist of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayyaḥ*).
The meaning is that they are established in the density of consciousness (*ciddhana*). Thus it has been said:
"The *mudrā* that moves in the space of consciousness is the *khecarī* state of Śiva.
The ten *mudrās*, beginning with *Śarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*, are the destroyers of fear, bestowers of supreme bliss, and the supreme powers."
This is the meaning. And so it has been said:

"Because they liberate the multitudes of bound souls from the seizing spirits and the like, and because they cause them to flow [toward liberation], they are therefore proclaimed as *mudrās* (seals)."

These mudrās, however, have been expounded by Paramaśiva as the presiding deities of the nine cakras, beginning with the square (caturaśra) and ending with the bindu; they are here illustrated merely by way of direction. For instance:
"The power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is consciousness (saṃvit) known as Ambikā, is called the mudrā of the universe."
Having assumed a three-part form, she is ever present nearby.

She is proclaimed as the pervader of the entire Cakrarāja; moreover, due to the abundance of the *yoni*, she is the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī (the All-Agitating One). Predominantly the power of Vāmā, she became established in the Wheel of the Gates (*dvāracakra*).
Beginning thus:
"Furthermore, this is the ground of enjoyment for the complete manifestation;
the Yonimudrā, whose form is the *kalā*, abides in that which consists of all-bliss."

That [point] should be understood from that very source. The *Yajuḥśruti* also states: "The lords of the wheels of the cows are of common origin; there are nine mudrās and nine wheels of the earth. This very point is explained by the passage beginning with "ādhāra": the ninefold foundation (*ādhāranavaka*) consists of Akula-sahasrāra, Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, Lambikā, A-jñā, and Bindu; these belong to her, who is the essential nature of the worshipper. For this reason, they constitute the nine wheels (*navacakratvena*).
By the cause that has transformed into the form of the *bindu*, the previously mentioned powers of the nine *nāthas* have become transformed into the form of the nine *mudrās*;
this is the meaning. And this has been explained in detail in the *Svacchandasaṅgraha*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. (46–47)
Its sevenfold [constituents] beginning with the skin, as well as its eightfold form, are clearly manifest;
this central mandala of the earth is presided over by the forms of the Mothers, Brāhmī and the others. 48.

The "cidvallī" (Creeper of Consciousness) refers to this Goddess’s sevenfold sheaths beginning with the skin—the seven bodily constituents such as the skin and so forth. Her form and her essential nature (*svarūpa*) constitute these eight aspects.
This means that she is the embodiment of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, that is, the essential nature of the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī. This is the visible orb of the central earth.
She dwells in, that is, resides within, the central square.
Her supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest, have assumed the form of lovely women;
being the fruits of other sciences (*vidyās*), they abide in the final earth as subordinate qualities. (49)

"Cidvallī" refers to the eight powers (aṣṭa-śaktayaḥ), beginning with *aṇimā*, of this Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvarī*). These powers have assumed the forms of lovely and enchanting women (*kāminī-rūpāṇi*)—the very fruits of other sciences such as Haṭha-yoga and others—which they have taken unto themselves. Being of such a nature, they exist in the state of a quality (*guṇa-bhāvena*), that is, in a subordinate capacity (*upasarjana-bhāvena*).

The meaning is that those residing in the final earthly abode remain within the final square. This is the sense: through such worship of the Supreme Self, the practitioner becomes the Supreme Lord. As it has been stated by the learned:
"Bearing His sovereignty, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others [attain their status]."
Those who possess sovereign power shine; that indeed is the Self, Sadāśiva.

Thus, having concluded the sequence of the *cakra* whose nature is the manifestation of the *kāmakalā*, [the author] begins to set forth the lineage of gurus beginning with Paramaśiva, out of a desire to favor his disciples, demonstrating that such a nature of the *mantra*s of the *cakradevatā*s is obtained through the realization of the knowledge of the lineage of gurus who are essentially the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

The supreme experience of bliss, whose essence is the particular *bindu* of the supreme Guru, further differentiated through its aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and in due course attained the state of Kāmeśa. (50)

From the words "cidvallī" and "paramānanda" up to "gurukramavidita," [the meaning is as follows]: He is one whose experience—his knowledge—is the supreme, most excellent bliss (*paramānanda*), which consists of the nature of the perfect sense of "I-ness" (*paripūrṇāhaṃbhāva*). This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Of this very bliss, other beings live on only a small portion."

"I bow to the Great Goddess, whose nature is supreme bliss"—so it is stated in the *Smṛti*. The Supreme Guru is the Lord who is non-different from the Bindu (the Point), the Supreme Guru Ādinātha, who is Paramaśiva. From that Ādinātha, he is "non-different" (*nirviśeṣa*). He is one whose form is the Self, the Bindu which is non-distinct [from him] and whose form is the previously mentioned *Kāmakalā*. The meaning is: Paramaśiva, whose form is Ādinātha. This is the sense: Bliss is Brahman...

Brahman is the supreme, infinite knowledge; it is pure consciousness, the seer of all, the witness of all, the grasper of all, the locus of all love, and the single essence of being, consciousness, and bliss. According to the method taught in the Upanishads, this very Self—consisting of pure being, eternal, pure, awakened, true, liberated, stainless, all-pervading, non-dual, and bliss—is the ultimate reality, a mass of consciousness and bliss.

The essential meaning is this: the Supreme Lord himself, whose nature is both light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), being supremely compassionate, has descended by his own will through the sequence of the divine couple—the forms of Kāmakalā and Bindu, and Kāma and Kāmeśvarī—along with the lineages of the divine, the Siddhas, and the human, manifesting as the assembly of Gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*). Thus, he protects those who possess devotion in this world. And this is heard in the *Rahasyopaniṣad*: "When she stepped forth... [yadeṣācakrame].
That became the wheel (*cakra*). That which was initially divided became the *bindu*; it became the support (*ādhāra*). This is the Self (*ātman*); this very power (*śakti*) is the Self;

she is both existence and non-existence, being and non-being. Thus say the teachers: "The one is not the worshiper; both belong to both. Both are born, yet both are eternal; they are one because of their inseparability (*avinābhāva*). They exist as the support and the supported. From that, the qualities (*guṇas*) are born. Those are the marks (*liṅgas*) and the bodies (*piṇḍas*); she became the power. On this point, there is also this verse:

"The *bindu* consists of both existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*); existence is enjoyment consisting of the six [faculties]. But that which is in its center, consisting of existence, is composed of the three beautiful states (*cārubhāva*). Thus it is said: "In the center, within the *bindu* of Śiva, is the wheel; therein is the world of manifestation (*prapañca*). The world is the body, whose nature is with resonance (*nāda*), and whose form is with sound (*śabda*)."

Power (*śakti*) consists of the object (*artha*). By means of the passage beginning with "The wheel is the body, the drop is the vital breath, and power is in the center," the essential nature of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī is described, preceded by a definition of the nature of the deities of the wheels (*cakradevatā*). Regarding this, it is said: "This is indeed the supreme bliss. She is the deity whose form is desire and who is the source of enjoyment. She is the source of bliss. Bliss is Brahman; being Brahman itself, one attains Brahman. One knows Brahman; one becomes Brahman itself."

It is so: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. By such statements as "Brahman is indeed the one and the manifold of the phenomenal world," the Goddess Kāmeśvarī is designated; and even at the conclusion, by the words "May that Mother of the world of Tripura, the Goddess who is of all forms, protect [us] always," the supremacy and the nature of being the self of all belonging to Kāmeśvarī are established. Thus, Paramaśiva alone is the protector of all. Or alternatively:
The word *paramaguruḥ* is to be split [as follows]: *paramaguruḥ* is Ādinātha. *Nirviśeṣaḥ* means devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*).
He is one whose essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) is the *bindu*, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
[This occurs] in the *baindava*, the supreme space (*paramākāśa*), which is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
In that which is free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, without discrimination, and without affliction.
Thus, from the words of Amṛtānanda; and also in the Rahasyāmnāya:
"Having entered that Śakti, you become condensed by means of Vāmā and the others;
enriched with the womb of all seeds, he attains the state of the subtle Bindu."
Also in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*: "The one who possesses the nature of the bindu and vimarśa is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the six paths.
Even the followers of Sāṅkhya and other schools are always *haṃsas*; with the eye of knowledge, they behold Mahādeva above the *nāda*, established within the *praṇava*.

With these words, the venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks of the Supreme Lord as consisting of *bindu* and *nāda*. He further states that the Supreme Lord, whose essence is such *bindu*, became the assembly of gurus headed by Kāma and Kāmeśvarī. Regarding the phrase "he, moreover, was subsequently divided," etc.:

"he" refers to the aforementioned Supreme Self (*paramātman*). "Subsequently" means he was brought to a state of dual form through the divisions of the divine and perfected forms to be described hereafter.

From the aspect of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which possesses the characteristics previously described, there arises His own power (*svātma-śakti*) in the form of *Kāmakalā*. A portion of that is its half-part.

For that reason, He attained the state of Kāmeśa—the condition of the venerable Kāmarāja. The meaning is this: the Supreme Self, having divided Himself, assumed the forms of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī and, entering into the relationship of teacher and disciple, set forth the entire Tantra.

And thus it is said in the Upaniṣad: "He split this very Self into two parts; from that, the husband and the wife came into being. [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1.4] "In the beginning, this was the Self alone, one only. He desired: 'May I have a wife, so that I may procreate. Thus, the Śruti declares that the single Brāhmaṇa possesses the nature of a couple. Furthermore, the Śruti itself states that for one who has become a couple, there is mastery over desire (kāmeśvaratva). As in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17]...

—"He for whom desire is the abode, the heart the world, and the mind the light—whosoever should know that person as the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, who is this very person consisting of desire (*kāmamaya*) that is to be established; that, Śākalya, is the divine one. "Which deity is his? "Women," he said. Thus [ends the section] concerning the Lord of Desire (*Kāmeśvara*).
He speaks directly to Kāmeśvarī, a woman worthy of dwelling [with him]: "And the Rahasyāgama states:
'The Guru, being Sadāśiva himself, abiding in the state of a disciple, brought down the Tantra for the sake of protecting the world. Thus.
This very point he clarifies: || 50 ||
Seated upon the Śrīpīṭha during the Kṛtayuga, Guru Śiva imparted the Vidyā to his own Śakti, Ekāṃśā, who is the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa) and possesses sovereign power.

Seated in the *Uḍyāṇa-pīṭha* located within the central triangle of the *Cidvallī-śrī-pīṭha*, the Guru—the instructor of knowledge—is eternally present. Thus it is said in the *Śivasūtra*: "To the one whose form is the Guru."
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* signifies that which dispels it;
because it obstructs darkness, it is designated as *guru*.

Śiva is the Supreme Self, the initiator of all. At the time of the Kṛta Yuga, at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, [he offers] to Her—to that Power who bestows limitless bliss upon all beings, to His own Śakti. In the *Rahasyopaniṣad* it is said: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Bhavānī—these are, in order, the transmitters of the tradition. Because she gives birth to all the worlds, she alone is Tripurā; she alone bestows bliss."

Also elsewhere it is said: "Even another who is devoid of power (*śakti*) is unable to do anything; O Supreme Goddess, one becomes endowed with power through power. According to the method stated in the *Saṅketapaddhati*: "The final letter *ha*, which is the form of the *kalā* (digit) and is called 'Vimarśa' (reflective awareness), is proclaimed [as such]. Thus, [salutation] to her whose supreme form is Power, the locus of repose in the unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānanda*), who bestows the tradition of one's own essential nature, and whose nature is Vimarśa.

She is Kāmā for the sake of the Mistress of Desire (Kāmeśvarī); she is all-desires, and desire itself is the worlds and the cities. Therefore, according to the method stated in the *Tripuropaniṣad*, she is "Tripurā. She is the bestower of all desired objects at all times and in every way. She is one who has become her own self; in other systems of knowledge, she is known as the Great Mantra (Mahāmanu).

That very Śabdā-tanu (the subtle body of Sound) is his supreme form, consisting of the same phonemes, designated as "three-footed," existing as the state of names, composed of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), having the nature of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), eternal, stainless, beyond phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcā*), the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*), all-pervading, and the most excellent knowledge. He who knows this becomes a wise man. Then they said: "The learned ones" means "the secret. "This is Śiva. He alone creates, protects, and destroys these beings; or he acts otherwise. "He alone becomes that"—thus [the teacher] bestowed and taught the ultimate knowledge of the Self, which grants the unity of the Self and is the subject matter of the *Rahasyopaniṣad*.

This is the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) here: although both [Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara] are equally principal and equal in essence, their power (*śakti*) is the source of the universe (*viśvayoni*), the primordial power (*ādiśakti*), Aruṇā, the mother of the universe (*viśvajanyā*). Thus, in the Sāṅkhyāyana Śākhā, it is stated that both Kāma and Kāmeśvarī are equally principal.

Nevertheless, because she is the source of the universe and the mother of the universe—being the embodiment of the cause of all—it is by this very Kāmeśvarī that the secret Tantra, which is the essence of all the Upaniṣads, [is revealed].
Desirous of setting [the teaching] in motion, the Supreme Śiva, immediately after the creation of the phenomenal world, in the primordial age—
[I] worship that which is the great center of the wheel, consisting of Great Bliss,
whose sole essence is unsurpassed reflective awareness, and which is composed of pure consciousness.

In the manner thus described, having established himself upon the seat of Oḍyāṇa—which consists of the essence of Light and Bliss—and bearing for himself the name Śrī Caryānanda, he taught the Krama of Śrīvidyā to the non-different Parābhaṭṭārikā. That Parābhaṭṭārikā, manifesting in the forms of the Gurus to be mentioned hereafter throughout the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas, set forth the most secret Śāmbhava Tantra. This is the sequence for the exposition of the Krama in this context.

In this regard, there are two lineages for the realization of the Śrīvidyā-ratna. The ancient gurus declare that the Kāmarāja lineage, which is the continuous transmission of the entire Vidyā, has been interrupted; they describe the Lopāmudrā lineage as being transmitted through a broken succession. The method of that lineage is now written down: therein, there are seven gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha) and four of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha).

There are eight gurus for the flood of humanity. Among them, the divine lineage (*divyakrama*) is as follows: At the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, Paramaśiva himself, residing in the central *bindu* which is the essence of the Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha, bearing the name Śrī Caryānandanātha, and having his body manifested through the contemplation of his own power known as Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, is the first guru. Thus it has been said: "She who dwells within the triangular Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha and possesses the body of Kāmarāja..."

"Having attained the state of formlessness, he emerged from the midst of the triangular convention. Thus, the venerable Ūrdhvadevanātha—the Guru of the Tretā Yuga—is the one whose form is contemplated as Kāmeśvarī, the presiding deity of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa at the Kāmarūpa Pīṭha, located at the foremost corner of the central triangle.
And so it has been said:
"She who resides at the front corner of the triangle is Kāmeśī, situated at the Kāma-pīṭha.

Thus, the venerable Lord Ṣaṣṭhanātha, the teacher of the Dvāpara age, is the embodiment of the union of Vajreśvarī—who resides at the Jālandhara-pīṭha located in the southern corner of the central triangle—and the one named Kāmarāja. As it has been said:
"Vajreśī, residing at the Jālandhara-pīṭha, is situated in the right corner of the central triangle. Thus it is said.

Śrī Mitradevanātha, the Guru of the Kali Yuga, whose body is contemplated as the Bhagamālinī—the one designated by the seed-syllable of Śakti—resides at the Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha, located in the northern corner of that same central triangle. And so it has been stated:
"Located in the northern corner of the triangle, Bhageśī resides at Pūrṇapīṭha. Thus [ends verse 51].
At the beginning of the Kali Yuga, Lord Mitreśadeva bestowed his grace upon the blessed Lopāmudrā and Agastya, a couple who were a mass of great asceticism.

These seven are to be understood as the group known as the Divine Current (divyaugha) through the instruction of the Guru; however, only this much has been stated here by way of context. He says this very thing:
"She too, he..."—referring to her [Lopāmudrā] and him [Agastya], who bear the name Mitra, and to the Lords of the Abodes (sthāneśas) known as the Elder, the Middle, and the Youth.
The three Gurus who are the causes of the Tretā Yuga and the other ages, who have become the objects of consciousness and vital breath.
Having examined the lords of the three seed-syllables, he revealed the Vidyā;
by these, the triad of lineages is fully embraced, and the succession of gurus is known. || 53 ||

"Cidvallī" refers to that aforementioned mistress of the life-force of Paramaśiva, known by the names Mitranātha and Devanātha. Just as in the expression "Bhīma" for Bhīmasena, the word *mitra* extends its application up to *mitradevanātha*. And that *mitradevanātha* is the Guru of the Kali age; his designation is his very name.

"Iyāya" means she arrived. This is also an elliptical expression; the meaning is that, having become the personification of the three *guru*s of the three ages beginning with the Tretā Yuga—namely, the Tretā Yuga, the Dvāpara Yuga, and the one bearing the name of the *Guru*—she shall set the tradition in motion. He explains this very point with the words "Sthāneśa," etc.:
Sthāneśa refers to Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī, who preside over the center, the eastern corner, the southern corner, and the northern corner of the [triangular] seats (*sthāna*).

She is the sovereign and presiding deity of the abodes; for this very reason, she is known by the names Jyeṣṭhā, Madhyā, and Bālā. Jyeṣṭha is the venerable Ūrdhvadevanātha; Madhya is the venerable Ṣaṣṭhadevanātha; and Bāla is the venerable Mitradevanātha. The sense is that she possesses their names and designations because she is their essential nature. She is the object of consciousness and vital breath; "consciousness and vital breath" refers to Paramaśiva, because he is both of the nature of consciousness and of the nature of the vital breath.

Likewise, in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad it is said: "They consider the Fourth (Turiya) to be neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both, neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, indefinable, the essence of the realization of the one Self, the cessation of the phenomenal world, auspicious, and non-dual. That is the Self; that is to be known. Thus, He is heard of as consisting of consciousness alone. Likewise, He is also heard of as consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya).
Likewise, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Just as the spokes are fixed in the nave, so in this Prāṇa everything is established.

Prāṇa moves by means of Prāṇa; Prāṇa gives Prāṇa; [one] gives to Prāṇa. Prāṇa is indeed the father, Prāṇa is the mother, Prāṇa is the brother, Prāṇa is the sister, and Prāṇa is the teacher. Thus, [the world] is the object and the object of enjoyment for Paramaśiva, whose essential nature is such consciousness-prāṇa.

"Why? Because this Lord is eternally eager for the flavor of play with this Goddess"—such is the statement of Abhinavaguptapāda. Alternatively, "the Lords of the [three] locations," namely those called the Eldest, the Middle, and the Child, who are the objects of consciousness and vital breath—this may be taken as an epithet of the Guru; even so, the meaning remains the same. Such is that Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā). [She is the cause of the Tretā age and so forth, the three Gurus beginning with the aforementioned venerable Ūrdhvadevanātha, and the triad of seeds.]

[The mantra] beginning with Vāgbhava; its presiding deities, who are its expressed meanings—this has already been stated previously. Having examined and purified these three kinds of teachers, [one should impart] the Vidyā—the universe consisting of the five elements, which is always identical with that [Vidyā], O sinless one.
And the root-vidyā consisting of that [essence]—I shall describe it to you in that same way.
He revealed—that is to say, he set in motion—the primordial Vidyā, which is the cause of all things and has issued forth from the lotus-face of Paramaśiva.

Regarding this, we shall say something: here, by the statement "having examined [the disciple], he revealed the Vidyā," it is understood that the supreme teacher, whose nature is Śrī Sadāśiva, practiced the worship of the Self for a long time according to this path established by the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*), and then instructed it to a self-controlled disciple who had approached him for instruction.

And: "O Maheśānī, the Guru should first instruct the Vidyā following initiation (dīkṣā)," and so forth. Furthermore, initiation bestows union with Śiva; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "It grants identity with Śiva and destroys the three impurities (malas);
therefore, by those who know the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*, it is called *dīkṣā*."

"For the contemplation of identity with Supreme Śiva is given, and the entire accumulation of sins is destroyed," according to the statement of the learned. And that [initiation] is threefold, due to the divisions of Āṇava, Śākta, and Sāmbhava. For it is stated in tradition: "That initiation is threefold; the first is Āṇavī, the other is Śākta, and the third is Sāmbhavī, which bestows immediate liberation."

In that regard, regarding the specific substances prescribed for the ritual procedure of the *āṇava* initiation, it is said: "The supreme deity is to be propitiated through offerings and meditation, having the form of one who is absorbed [in the practice].
As for the *śākteyī* [initiation], however, it is to be accomplished by means of whatever power (*śakti*) is available. And as for the *śāmbhavī*:
"Having perceived the power established in the disciple, by that alone..."
"The initiation pertaining to Śakti is said to be performed without [external] means.
Thus, even without a formal agreement between both teacher and disciple,
the manifestation of Śiva-nature occurs solely through the grace of the Guru.
"For this very Śāmbhavī initiation is that which causes entry into Śiva. And thus:
"In the absence of such an initiation, there is no qualification for anything whatsoever. Accordingly, the author of the *Śrīmālinīvijaya* says:
"Without initiation, there is no eligibility for Yoga in the tradition of Śaṅkara."
Nor is eligibility for yoga restricted to the Śāmbhava alone.

"If this [initiation] should occur through the mere compassion of the teacher, devoid of any ulterior motive, then even the qualification for mantras is said to be attained through Śiva-initiation. Thus, even in the absence of wealth from the disciple, the teacher, having ascertained the disciple's fitness, may perform [the rite] with his own wealth; or, if he too lacks it, he may do so by an easy means.
"The Guru himself should perform initiation for a poor person using his own wealth."
Or else, one may liberate the child by means of dūrvā grass and water, or through initiation.

Thus, the established conclusion is that only one who has been initiated in every respect (*sarvātmanā*) is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and no other. It has been stated that initiation (*dīkṣā*) is to be accomplished by the propitiation of the Supreme Deity (*paradevatā*). And this propitiation consists of a specific offering of liquid substances (*dravadravya*) appropriate to the particular age (*yuga*), which bestows satisfaction (*tṛpti*);
for it is said: "But with the nectar of the Deity. For this very reason, it is said: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very [Self] through the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*)."
"By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting. Since sacrifice also has Brahman as its object, it is stated in scripture:
"That sacrifice is worship, and it is considered to be threefold: the higher (parā), the lower (aparā), and the intermediate (parāparā). And thus Paramaśiva spoke to the Supreme Goddess:
Your eternally manifest worship is established in three divisions:
the supreme (parā), the non-supreme (aparā), O Gaurī, and the third, which is both supreme and non-supreme (parāparā).
The first state, abiding in non-duality, is the sphere of all that is most excellent;
and the second, the worship of the wheel, is always performed by me.
Thus, O Goddess, in that which consists of knowledge, the third is both the higher-lower (parāparā) and the supreme (uttama); she is to be known as the highest (parā). Now hear the ritual procedure.

One should contemplate the Guru’s sandals within the Vāgbhava syllable— the Goddess who resides at the edge of the Great Lotus Grove, whose form is the bliss of the Cause, and who rests upon his limbs.
Having meditated upon her who nourishes the form of the universe and showers supreme nectar, one should drink from the vessel of the intoxication of the realization of supreme non-duality.
Intent upon illumination through contact with another flame,
he is always turned away from conceptual thought and the will for worldly objects, facing inward.
The movement of consciousness is charmingly contracted by its own delight; it is exceedingly beautiful, performing its own worship through substances that gratify the senses.
O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), preceded by the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Such is the supreme worship (*parā pūjā*). Regarding this, within the essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is said:
"And the second, the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*), is always performed by me.
Paramaśiva himself, existing externally, praised the worship of the wheel, saying, "I perform the service (*varivasyā*). He too—

The external sacrifice is fivefold—*kevala*, *yāmala*, *miśra*, *cakrayuk*, and *vīrasaṅkara*—according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*). Its specific characteristics are to be understood from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) alone. Therefore, rites such as consecration (*abhiṣecana*) and the like must be performed only after first performing the act of satiation (*santarpaṇa*).

And it has been stated that this substance for satiation must be prepared. Furthermore, the liquid substance—which serves as the causal basis, the source, and the primary cause denoted by terms such as "first" and so forth—is honey in the form of supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*). This is because the sacrifice to the Supreme Deity is accomplished by that alone, just as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is performed with Soma. Nor should it be argued that [the use of liquor] is improper because of the existence of injunctions such as, "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agniṣṭoma," or "One should draw the Soma cups. It is indeed appropriate.

It has been stated that other sacrifices are accomplished through *soma*. However, one might argue that this present vision is untenable because of prohibitions such as "A Brahmin shall not drink *surā* (liquor)" and "He shall not eat meat. We do not say that it is appropriate to perform the propitiation of the Supreme Deity independently, by transgressing the prohibitive injunctions. Rather, we maintain that this very Śāmbhava vision has descended from the Upaniṣadic tradition.

Having determined this, we have indeed spoken thus. If it is asked, "What then is the status of the prohibition? it is replied: this injunction of prohibition concerns an uninitiated person (*adīkṣita-puruṣa*).

For one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*), by this very reason, the sacrifice to the deity must be performed; since there exists a primary injunction (*mukhya-vidhi*) to that effect. And so, in the Śāṅkhāyana Śākhā, which has been drawn from the midst of the ocean of the Ṛgveda, [there is] the means for achieving the sovereignty of the deity through the *Ādisundarī-vārivasyā*.
It is heard:
having known this, the gods rejoice; overflowing, they satisfy their own seat;
they dwell upon the back of the great heaven and enter the supreme abode of Tripura.

In this context, the meaning is "the substance that has been poured out. This is well-established in the *Nighaṇṭu* and other such works. For this very reason, even in well-known sacrifices such as the *Vājapeya*, the acceptance of substances—even those otherwise prohibited—is observed, precisely because the Supreme Goddess, the Mistress of Mantras, is enjoined therein. Where else is the injunction for the Supreme Goddess heard? And in the *Lalitopākhyāna*:
I am well-pleased with you, O Ocean; you have rendered me supreme assistance. You have ensured that this certain task of the gods was accomplished free from obstacles.
Henceforth, by my grace, in sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and others, [you shall attain success].
You will become one who consumes [it] excessively, like the drinking of soma.
In sacrifices, all the deities shall drink you, purified by mantras;
and by drinking you, who have been purified by the sacrifice, people [shall attain their goals].

"May Maheśvarī, Mahādeva, Baladeva, Bhārgava, Dattātreya, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these great beings—bestow upon you success, supernatural power, strength, heaven, and liberation; may they protect you. Thus [it is said].

Even Paramaśiva, in the context of the conventions of worship, speaks of her as having brought about the state of being superior to Pradhāna and the rest. Or, for example: "In the forest of Mahāpadma, within the embodiment of the bliss of the Cause, [I behold] the Goddess, who bestows the fruits of desire and will, resting upon my lap."
One should worship you with offerings such as food (naivedya) that consist of nothing but your own essence.
Having spoken thus from the beginning, he clearly describes the substance for the food offering at the end. For example:
"Having worshipped the deity with meat, perfumes, and incense, and having performed the worship of the circle (cakrapūjā) in this manner, one should offer the Kula-lamp."
One should perform worship together with heroes who are endowed with the Kaulika conduct.
In another secret scripture (*rahasyāgama*), the Supreme Lord speaks of the five deities of the first group of five categories: "O Īśānī, the first pentad brings about the pleasure of the deity.

Now, one might object: "Is it not Śiva alone who is the independent initiator? To this, it has been stated in the *Mahāmāyā*, *Śāmbara*, and many other tantras regarding their practice: [the following].

If it is argued that this leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), [we reply: having stated that, [one might say] "no, because of the distinction"; for those tantras are to be practiced according to the specific differences among their respective qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*).
However, in this case, the Śāmbhava vision is to be worshipped only by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), as has been explained at length. As it is said:
"All the delusive scriptures (*mohaśāstra*) have indeed been proclaimed by me alone."
Having gone into the midst of the liberated ones, however, for the purpose of deluding the evil-minded.
Having spoken thus—
O Goddess, having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Agamas with the churning-stick of knowledge, I, who am a knower of the essence, have extracted the Kula-dharma.
O Mother, just as there is a vast difference between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly,
so too is the difference between my own lineage and that of other families.
Having thus described the essential nature of the Kula system, he states that liberation belongs only to one established therein, and not to one established in other systems:
"O fair lady, having known this, one immediately attains the state of moving through the sky;
this is the play of the woman who is the digit of desire (Kāmakalā), arisen from the bliss of merit."
The serpent of supreme Śiva is ever capable of bringing joy through the attraction of all states of being. || 54 ||

Salutations to that illustrious Lord, the navigator, by whose grace I have crossed the ocean of conceptual proliferation, which has the internal thoughts as its waves and the thirst for existence as its waters. 55.
Regarding the phrase "arisen from the *cidvallī*": it has arisen—that is, been produced—from its own source called Puṇyānanda. This is the play (*vilāsa*) of the woman who is Kāmakalā.

Kāmakalā is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) which is inseparable from Kāmeśvara; she herself is the beautiful woman (*aṅganā*), and her play consists of the forms of the deities of the wheels (*cakra*) and their enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).

That very *vilāsa* (graceful play) is the transformation of the mind occurring at that moment when the beloved is beheld. Paraśiva is the serpent whose sole nature is light; he is the connoisseur (*rasika*) and the gallant (*viṭa*). His *bhāva* is the excellence born of joy; it is what is meant by "overflowing grace" (*udvilāsa*). Such [grace] is fit for—that is, capable of—bestowing *harṣa*, which is bliss. Regarding the alternative reading *bhāvākarṣaṇaharṣāya*: from that [beholding], there is the drawing forth (*ākarṣaṇa*), or the arising, of *bhāva*.

By that [beauty], the joy (*harṣa*) which is produced; the specific internal transformation (*vikāraviśeṣa*) arising through the playful glance (*vilāsekṣaṇa*) is the emotion (*bhāva*). By means of that, the playfulness (*vilāsa*) is brought forth; the meaning is that it becomes a cause of joy by way of generating the emotion. Even in the world, upon seeing the most exquisite playfulness, joy arises in a connoisseur hero (*rasikanāyaka*), preceded by the emergence of the erotic emotion (*śṛṅgārabhāva*). In the same way, for Paraśiva, who is oriented toward the vision of his own power (*ātma-śaktīkṣaṇābhimukhya*), there is the playfulness of the *kāmakalā*, which is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

It bestows infinite bliss in the form of the movement of his feet and so forth. This *Kāmakalāvilāsa*, which has emerged from the lotus of his own mouth in the form of an Āryā verse and exists as a literary work, serves as a means for attaining the grace of Paraśiva. It is understood that the great soul, whose nature is the bliss of merit arising from the experience of the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*, speaks thus.
The word "iti" (thus) should be understood as indicating the completion [of the work]. That which has been studied but not realized in its true meaning is like the braying of a donkey.

For it is heard from the words of the authors of the *Nirukta* and others that study devoid of knowledge of the meaning is as fruitless as carrying a load of sandalwood that results only in exhaustion:
"The meaning of all the Vedas must be known for the accomplishment of ritual acts;
one who has studied the Vedas merely by rote perishes like a cow stuck in the mud."
Indeed, all study of the Veda and of the Dharmaśāstra by one who does not understand their meaning is like the threshing of chaff.

Thus, the nature of Kāmakalā, established by such scriptural passages as these, has been fully and elaborately explained. May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends the commentary on the *Kāmakalā-cidvallī* composed by Śrī Naṭanānanda.
May this be offered at the lotus feet of the venerable Guru.
May this be offered to Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.
